### Story timeline (opt-in)

The headliner of the cycle and the biggest single
feature. Off by default — enable via
`timeline.enabled: true`.

```hjson
timeline: {
  enabled: true
  default_track: "main"
  calendar: { preset: "gregorian" }    # or "sols" / "custom"
}
```

Three preset shapes. Custom calendars define their own
unit stack (e.g. 30-day months + 12-month years), named
months, seasons, epoch labels, and a format string. The
parser infers precision from the input shape — `1A` is
year-precision, `1A.3` is month, `1A.spring` is season
(90-day window), `1A.3.15` is day. Negative ticks for
prequels.

**CLI:**

```

inkhaven event list --book-name "Aerin Saga" --track main
inkhaven event show aerin-saga/timeline/storm
```

A `Timeline` chapter materialises lazily inside the
target book on first `event add`. Tagged
`system_tag: book_timeline` so renames don't break it.

**TUI:**

```
Ctrl+V e         chronological event picker (track filter, t/T)
Ctrl+V Shift+E   new event from any pane — opens timeline and

                 fresh project (no chicken-and-egg with the CLI)
Ctrl+V Shift+T   swim-lane view — scope-aware, auto-fits the
                 full event span on open
Ctrl+V Shift+I   edit the open event's start | end | track

```

Inside Ctrl+V Shift+T:

```
↑ / ↓     hop cursor to prev / next event (chronological)
← / →     scroll viewport (~10 cells)
PgUp/PgDn page-scroll (~60 cells)
+/-       zoom in / out          0       reset zoom
Home/End  jump first / last
Tab       cycle highlighted track
Enter     open event nearest cursor
n         new event at cursor tick

u / U     up-scope               b       jump to book scope
d / D     descent picker         p       toggle project overlay
y         critique current track-and-scope
Y         critique current scope (all tracks)
Ctrl+Y    book-wide critique (all tracks)
```

Scope: events at sub-book scope are filtered by their
`linked_paragraphs` — an event appears iff itself OR any
of its linked paragraphs sits in the current subtree.
Orphan events render with `◌`.

**AI critique** (y/Y/Ctrl+Y) builds a flat-text payload

mismatches, fuzzy-precision overlaps, orphan signals,
and pacing outliers. Custom prompt: rename

**Bund:** seven `ink.event.*` words —
`list / list_orphans / add / set_end / set_precision /
set_track / link_paragraph`. Two new hooks:
`hook.on_event_added ( uuid -- )` (fires on every add)
and `hook.on_event_orphaned ( uuid -- )` (fires on
linked → orphan transition).

release.  Two themes carry the branch:

1. **Timeline + ergonomics polish.**  The story timeline

   navigation, a recent-¶ picker, mouse-capture toggle for

   watcher that detects when CLI / sed / git pull touched
   the open paragraph.
2. **Internal architecture rework.**  `src/tui/app.rs` —
   the editor's TUI brain — went from a 26,605-LOC monolith
   to a 13,939-LOC central dispatcher with 21 sibling /
   child modules hanging off it (text helpers, modal +
   state types, splash painters, render dispatcher with
   modal / pane painter sub-modules, 8 `impl App` domain
   splits).  Pure refactor — every commit byte-equivalent
   modulo visibility / paths, verified by a programmatic

intentionally short — bug reports from real users surface
slowly, and this cycle's bandwidth went to ergonomics +

## Headline changes

### Timeline — six polish refinements

The 1.2.6 swim lanes shipped with single-Tab navigation
through tracks and no persistence.  1.2.7 layered:

- **Two-level Tab/Enter navigation** mirroring the tree pane.
  Tab cycles tracks; Enter expands a track into a text
  sub-row of its events; Tab inside the expansion cycles
  events in chronological order; Enter on an event opens
  the LinkPicker modal over its linked paragraphs.  Esc /
  Backspace pops back up.
- **Track collapse** with `Space`.  Collapsed tracks render
  as `▸ track-name · N events`; expanded ones as full swim
  lanes prefixed `▾`.
- **Span-aware event selection.**  `↑` / `↓` pick the
  previous / next event by start tick AND highlight every
  cell carrying that event id.  Viewport auto-pans so both
  `start_ticks` and `end_ticks` are visible — duration
  events read clearly even when zoomed in.
- **Grid stripes.**  Every Nth column gets a faint dotted
  backdrop so the eye has something to register against at
  wide zoom.  N follows the visible span (weeks at day
  zoom, years at month zoom).
- **`F12` full-book critique** from inside the timeline
  view.  Same payload as `Ctrl+Y` (book-wide health check)

- **Quick-event from selection.**  `Ctrl+V Shift+E` reads
  the editor selection, the tree paragraph title, or the
  timeline cursor — whatever's contextually present — and
  pre-fills the new-event prompt with it.  Two chords to
  drop a calendar event for the scene under the cursor.
- **Book-slug prefix** in the project overlay (`p` chord).
  Cross-book tracks now render as `aerin-saga/main` vs
  `khaal-arc/main` instead of two ambiguous rows called
  `main`.

Session persistence captures the per-book view state in
`.session.json`: collapsed tracks, expanded track, track
highlight, zoom, scroll tick, cursor tick.  Re-opening the
timeline for the same book restores all six.

See [`Tutorials/31-story-timeline.md`](../Tutorials/31-story-timeline.md)
"1.2.7 polish".

### Paragraph undelete (Ctrl+B U)

A single-slot kill-ring for paragraph deletions.  After a
Ctrl+D delete-confirm, `Ctrl+B U` restores the paragraph at
its original position, with body, tags, status,
linked-paragraph cross-refs, and event timing intact.  The
restored paragraph gets a fresh uuid; the status bar is
upfront that incoming wiki-links to the old uuid stay
broken.

The slot is single-paragraph only — branch deletes (chapter
/ subchapter / book) can't be undone and clear the slot
when they fire.  Session-local; restart starts empty.

See [`Tutorials/32-paragraph-undelete.md`](../Tutorials/32-paragraph-undelete.md).

### Visited-paragraph history (Alt+← / Alt+→ + Ctrl+V Shift+P)

Browser-style back / forward across every code path that
opens a paragraph: tree Enter, fuzzy picker, bookmark
picker, wiki-link follow, snapshot picker, similar-¶
picker, timeline Enter, undelete.

```
Alt+←           step backward through visited paragraphs
Alt+→           step forward (after stepping back)
Ctrl+V Shift+P  recent-paragraph picker (most-recent-first list,
                up to 32 entries)
```

Opening a NEW paragraph (anything not Alt+→) clears the
forward stack — same as a web browser.  Ring is in-memory
only; restart clears it.

See [`Tutorials/33-navigation-history.md`](../Tutorials/33-navigation-history.md).

### Mouse capture toggle (Ctrl+Shift+M)

`Ctrl+Shift+M` flips between two modes:

- **Capture ON** (the default): click-to-focus, scroll-wheel
  per-pane, in-TUI drag-select.
- **Capture OFF**: the terminal handles drag-select; the
  terminal's native copy keystroke (Cmd+C on macOS,
  Ctrl+Shift+C on Linux) copies the highlight to the
  system clipboard.  Useful for grabbing a snippet to paste
  elsewhere, or copying mid-stream AI output without
  routing through the Ctrl+C selection-mode chord-flow.

Session-only; defaults to ON every fresh launch.

### External-change auto-reload

Once per autosave tick (every keystroke + idle timer)
the editor checks whether the open paragraph's file changed
on disk.  Three behaviours:

- **mtime unchanged**: no-op.
- **mtime newer, buffer clean**: silent reload + status
  `↻ reloaded …`.  Cursor jumps to (0, 0) since the previous
  position may not survive an external rewrite.
- **mtime newer, buffer dirty**: red warning, buffer
  untouched: `⚠ <title> changed on disk while you have
  unsaved edits — Ctrl+S to overwrite the external change`.

Triggers: `inkhaven event add` (events live as paragraphs),
`sed -i`, `git pull`, another instance of the TUI, Bund
scripts that mutate paragraph files.  Cost: one
`std::fs::metadata().modified()` per tick — cheap.

See [`Tutorials/34-mouse-and-external-changes.md`](../Tutorials/34-mouse-and-external-changes.md).

### Snapshot dedupe

The F5 / autosave snapshot pipeline drops a new snapshot
when the buffer content matches the previous snapshot's
content.  Avoids growing the F6 picker with duplicate rows
when nothing meaningful changed (common during status
toggles, metadata-only edits, and the autosave loop firing
on a clean buffer).

The dedupe is content-based — annotation differences alone
don't create a new snapshot if the body is byte-identical.

### F8 from any pane

The typst-diagnostics list modal previously needed editor
focus.  In 1.2.7 it works from tree, AI, and search panes
too — opens against the most-recently-active paragraph's
cached diagnostics.

### today widget gets colour

The status-bar "today: N/M words" widget now colours by
goal progress:

- red `<25%` of goal
- yellow `25–75%`
- green `≥75%`
- bold-green when goal-hit / exceeded

Visual nudge without taking up more status-bar real estate.

## Fixes

- **Ctrl+S no longer jumps the cursor to (0, 0).**  Pre-
  existing bug since the 1.2.7 external-change auto-reload
  landed: `save_current` wrote the file but never restamped
  `doc.loaded_mtime`, so the next autosave tick saw the
  fresh mtime, considered it an external edit, and silently
  reloaded the buffer.  The reload path resets the cursor.
  Fixed by adding the same three-line restamp `save_doc`
  already had.  Surface symptom — every Ctrl+S snapped the
  cursor home — is gone.
- **`src/export/markdown.rs:166` duplicate-comparison.**
  `trimmed == ")" || trimmed == ")"` was a copy-paste
  artifact — the second operand identical to the first.
  Collapsed to the single comparison the runtime already
  evaluated.  No behaviour change; clippy was failing on
  the binary because of it.
- **5 environment-gated tests now run in CI.**  The
  story-view + typst-render + typst-inprocess end-to-end
  smoke tests previously carried `#[ignore]` because typst

  `libfontconfig1-dev` (headers) but no fonts.  CI now
  installs `fonts-dejavu-core`; `#[ignore]` removed; doc

(`Ctrl+Z o`) and the **in-TUI HJSON config editor**

### Embedded nushell pane

`Ctrl+Z o` opens a floating shell inside the TUI window.
Runs **real nushell** in-process via `nu_engine` +
`nu_command` — the full default command set (`ls`, `where`,
`str`, `path`, `into`, pipelines, env mutations) without
shelling out.  Output of any command can be selected
(`Ctrl+Z h` enters selection mode, ↑↓ walks turns) and
either `c` copied to clipboard or `i` inserted into the
editor wrapped as a typst `#raw(block: true, …)` block
(template HJSON-configurable).

```
Ctrl+Z o    open / close (engine + history preserved)
Ctrl+Z O    open fresh (drop cached engine + ring)
Ctrl+Z h    inside the pane, toggle selection mode
PgUp/PgDn   scroll the turn buffer (10 lines/press)
Shift+Home  jump to top of buffer
Shift+End   jump back to newest output
```

External command output is **captured**, not inherited —
`^/bin/ls -l`, `^git status`, … all route their stdout +
stderr through a `Stack::push_redirection(Pipe, Pipe)` guard
so the bytes land inside the pane instead of escaping into
the ratatui alternate-screen surface.  Stderr is **merged
into stdout** (the `Pipe`-on-both contract), so a failing
`^/bin/ls /nonexistent` surfaces its `No such file or
directory` message in the pane like a real terminal —
including when the external exits non-zero, because the
captured ChildProcess has `ignore_error=true` flipped on
it before draining so the bytes survive the exit-code
check.  Per-turn output is capped at `shell.max_output_lines`
lines (default 1000) so a single `git log` doesn't bloat
the buffer; excess tail is replaced with a `… (N more lines
truncated)` marker.

Layout polish: short turn buffers (a single `ls` in a
fresh session) now anchor to the **bottom** of the pane
just above the prompt, instead of floating at the top of
a 60-row body with a huge empty gap between output and
prompt.  Long buffers that exceed the body height
continue to scroll normally.  When NOT scrolled, the
render also clamps the visible window's top to the
start of the most-recent turn — so after a `help
commands` (truncated to 1000 lines) followed by `ls`,
the `ls` output appears alone at the bottom instead of
sharing the screen with the tail of the help output.
PgUp brings the older turns back into view.

Typing `exit` or `quit` at the shell prompt closes the
pane (terminal muscle memory) rather than forwarding to
nu's `exit` built-in, which would call
`std::process::exit()` and take the whole editor down
with it.  Any trailing args are ignored — `exit 1`,
`quit`, `exit anything` all close the pane.

**Readline-style line editing.**  The shell prompt now
honours the chord set familiar to bash / zsh users:
`Ctrl+A` / `Ctrl+E` for start / end of line; `Ctrl+U` /
`Ctrl+K` for kill-to-start / kill-to-end; `Ctrl+W` to
kill the previous word; `Ctrl+Left` / `Ctrl+Right` and
`Alt+B` / `Alt+F` for word-wise motion; `Alt+Backspace`
for kill-word-back; `Ctrl+L` to clear the scrollback
(engine + history preserved); `Ctrl+D` to clear input
(or close the pane when input is empty).  Hyphens stay
word-chars so `--short` counts as one logical token.

**Colored prompt.**  Replaced the bare `$ ` prefix with
`[ <cwd> > ` — `[` in white, `<cwd>` in blue (`$HOME`
abbreviated to `~`, tracking `cd`), `>` in red.  Input
after the `>` keeps the existing syntax-highlight pass
from nu's flat-shape tokeniser.

**Ctrl+B H in-pane help.**  A 40-line overlay describes
line-editing chords, pane chords, sample nu commands,
and a one-paragraph orientation about what the
embedded shell is and isn't.  Any key dismisses the
overlay; pane state is preserved unchanged underneath.

**Tab autocomplete.**  Tab in the pane prompt completes
the token under the cursor.  In command position (start
of input or after `|` / `;` / `(`) it matches nu's
declared command set (all built-ins + any `def`s the
user has made this session) **plus** executables on
`$PATH`.  In argument position (and for any
command-position token containing `/`) it matches
filesystem entries under the engine's current working
directory; directories come back with a trailing `/`
so a second Tab can walk into them.  Single match →
splice into input + trailing space; multiple → splice
the longest common prefix and list candidates on the
status bar (`shell: 5 matches — string  str  ...`).

**Full-screen TUI safety net** (three layers):

- *Blocklist.*  A pre-spawn check against
  `shell.blocked_externals` refuses commands whose
  basename matches a known full-screen app — `vim`,
  `nvim`, `less`, `top`, `htop`, `tmux`, `mc`, `fzf`,
  `ssh`, `gdb`, `psql`, `sudo`, … (default ~45 entries,
  fully HJSON-configurable).  Case-insensitive,
  basename-matched, so `^vim`, `^/usr/bin/vim`, `^VIM`
  all hit.  The user gets a clear "blocked: `vim` is a
  full-screen TUI app and would corrupt the editor's
  alt-screen surface" message and the engine is left
  untouched.
- *Null stdin.*  The embedded engine sets
  `EngineState::is_mcp = true`, which causes nu's
  external runner to spawn children with
  `Stdio::null()` for stdin instead of inheriting our
  TTY.  Apps that respect `isatty(STDIN_FILENO)`
  (well-behaved REPLs, password prompts, most
  cooperative TUIs) fail-fast.  Doesn't stop apps that
  open `/dev/tty` directly — that's what the blocklist
  is for.
- *Wall-clock watchdog.*  Every eval runs in a worker
  thread; the main thread polls with
  `shell.external_timeout_secs` (default 30s).  On
  timeout, nu's interrupt signal fires; if the worker
  responds within a 2-second grace window, the engine
  is recovered cleanly.  If the worker stays wedged
  (vim blocking on `/dev/tty` despite signal), the
  engine is **rebuilt from scratch** — env vars / `def`
  declarations / `cd`-mutated `$env.PWD` are lost, but
  the TUI stays responsive.  The user sees a status
  message explaining what happened and how to add the
  offending binary to the blocklist.

Per-project SQLite history at
`<project>/.inkhaven/shell_history.db` — survives restart.
Engine state (env vars, defs) survives modal close + reopen.
Configurable via HJSON: `shell.enabled` (default true),
`shell.max_buffered_turns` (default 50),
`shell.max_output_lines` (default 1000),
`shell.insert_template` (default typst raw block).

Out of scope (deliberate): long-running TTY apps (`vim`,
`top`, `less`), reedline integration, plugins.  This is for
one-shot pipelines whose output you want to capture or
inspect — not a full terminal emulator.  Use a separate
terminal for interactive workflows.

Binary size: +18M (103→121M end-to-end across the seven
shell-phase commits), of which ~13M is rusqlite's bundled
SQLite and ~5M is nu's core + standard command set.  LTO
+ strip aggressively trim nu's built-ins we don't reach
via runtime dispatch.  See
[`Tutorials/35-embedded-shell.md`](../Tutorials/35-embedded-shell.md).

# Inkhaven 1.2.9 — Prose-craft tools for novelists

1.2.9 turns inkhaven from a *book editor* into a
*book editor that audits your prose while you write
it*.  Nine new features, all keyed to the same
writing-craft idea: catch the mechanical weaknesses
(drone, telling, hedging, lexical ruts) inline,
while the words are still soft, instead of
discovering them at revision time.

The headline overlays (always-on, zero latency):

  * **Filter-word highlight** (`Ctrl+B Shift+F`) —
    intensifier crutches + hedges, stemmed,
    multilingual (English / Russian / French /
    German / Spanish).
  * **Repeated-phrase detector** — n-gram window
    flags writer-crutch gestures (`lifted her
    shoulders` matching `lifting her shoulders`)
    via Snowball stemming.
  * **Show-don't-tell flag** — copula + emotion-
    adjective 2-grams, manner-of-emotion adverbs,
    cognition verbs.

On-demand modals + chips:

  * **Concordance view** (`Ctrl+B Shift+L`) —
    project-wide lexical fingerprint with KWIC
    samples.
  * **Sentence-rhythm gauge** (`Ctrl+B Shift+H`) —
    measures the felt rhythm of the prose, mapped
    against Gary Provost's "this sentence has five
    words" parable.
  * **POV / character chip** (`Ctrl+B Shift+P`) —
    status-bar surfaces the heuristic POV character
    + supporting cast, driven by the existing
    characters lexicon.
  * **Writing-streak heatmap** (`Ctrl+B Shift+G`) —
    GitHub-style 91-day word-activity grid.
  * **Scene-break navigation** (`Ctrl+B <` /
    `Ctrl+B >`) — jump between typographic dividers
    inside the open paragraph.

Accessibility:

  * **Text-to-speech read-aloud** (`Ctrl+B S`) +
    **save as audio** (`Ctrl+B Shift+R`) — provides
    the *ear* feedback that catches what the eye
    glides over.

AI-augmented:

  * **AI show-don't-tell scan** (`Ctrl+B Shift+T`) —
    sends the open paragraph to the configured LLM
    with a system prompt asking for telling phrases
    plus concrete rewrites.

Each feature has its own detail section below.

### Show-don't-tell flag — inline overlay + AI scan

Two complementary layers for catching prose that
*tells* the reader an emotion instead of *showing*
it through behaviour, sensory detail, dialogue, or
action.

**Layer 1: regex-based inline overlay** (always-on,
zero latency, instant feedback while typing)

A new `ShowDontTellDetector` joins the filter-word
and repeated-phrase detectors under the
`Ctrl+B Shift+F` style-warnings toggle.  Tokens
matched by any of three patterns get a teal
underline:

  1. **Copula + emotion adjective** — a 2-gram
     `(linking_verb)(emotion_adjective)` where the
     verb is `be` / `is` / `are` / `was` / `were` /
     `seem` / `feel` / `appear` / `look` / `become`
     / `remain` / `grow` / `sound` (stemmed) and the
     adjective is one of ~70 curated emotion lemmas
     (`angry`, `sad`, `happy`, `afraid`, …).  Both
     tokens flagged.
  2. **Manner-of-emotion adverbs** — single
     `-ly` adverbs that label emotion outright
     (`angrily`, `sadly`, `nervously`, `wearily`, …).
  3. **Cognition verbs** — single verbs that tell
     the reader the character's interior directly
     (`realised`, `understood`, `knew`, `wondered`,
     `decided`, …).

Hits emit `StyleWarningKind::ShowDontTell` with a
new theme colour `style_warning_show_dont_tell_fg`
(default soft teal `#94e2d5`) — distinct from
filter-word amber + repeated-phrase magenta so the
three overlays stay visually separate when
adjacent.

Patterns are stemmed via the project's Snowball
algorithm so inflections collapse: `seemed`/`seems`/
`seeming` all match the same `seem` linking-verb
stem.  Per-language scaffold ships with English
defaults populated; Russian / French / German /
Spanish lists start empty so the user can fill them
in for the corpus they write in (emotion vocabulary
varies enough per genre and language register that
shipping a default for, say, Russian prose would
mislead more than help).

False-positive control: `was running`, `was reading`,
`looks at the door` — none flagged, because the
2-gram requires both halves to match.  `He was
angry` flags both `was` and `angry`; `He was angry
about something` flags only `was angry`.

**Layer 2: AI-driven scan** (`Ctrl+B Shift+T`)

Sends the open paragraph to the configured LLM
with a system prompt asking for:

  1. Every telling phrase, quoted.
  2. The emotion / state being told.
  3. One concrete show-rewrite per instance.

Response streams into the AI pane.  Reuses the
existing `Inference` plumbing — same patterns as
F12 critique + grammar check.  The prompt name is
`show-dont-tell`; users can override via the
project's prompts book or the global prompts.hjson
the same way they override critique prompts.

Why both layers?  The regex catches the obvious
2-grams (`was angry`, `realised`) instantly while
the writer is still typing.  The AI scan catches
subtler instances — declarative statements,
adverb-modified verbs the regex misses, narration
that explains rather than dramatises — and proposes
specific rewrites.  Together they cover the cheap
loop and the deep loop.

Config (`inkhaven.hjson`):

```hjson
editor: {
  style_warnings: {
    enabled: true
    show_dont_tell: {
      enabled: true
      use_stemming: true
      // English defaults populated automatically;
      // override per language by filling in the
      // per-language lists.
      english_emotion_adjectives: []
      english_cognition_verbs: []
      // … etc.
    }
  }
}
```

Mnemonic: `Shift+T` for *tell* — the AI chord.

### Sentence-rhythm gauge (`Ctrl+B Shift+H`)

A modal that quantifies the rhythm of the open
paragraph and surfaces the felt monotony / variety of
the prose.  Inspired by Gary Provost's well-known
parable:

> "This sentence has five words.  Here are five more
> words.  Five-word sentences are fine.  But several
> together become monotonous.  Listen to what is
> happening.  The writing is getting boring."

What the gauge measures:

  * Splits the paragraph into sentences with a hand-
    rolled walker.  Recognised terminators: `.`,
    `!`, `?` followed by whitespace.  Suppresses
    splits inside common abbreviations (Mr., Mrs.,
    Dr., Sr., Jr., Prof., e.g., i.e., Ph.D., M.D.,
    etc., Inc., Ltd., …).  Treats `...` / `....` as
    a mid-sentence pause, not a terminator.
    Consumes trailing closing quotes + parens so
    `said "Hello."` is one sentence, not two.
  * Tokenises each sentence with the same UAX-#29
    word segmenter that powers the concordance, so
    word counts are consistent across features.
  * Reports per-sentence word count, plus the
    aggregate: mean, population stdev, coefficient
    of variation (CV = stdev / mean).
  * Maps CV to a discrete verdict (with text note
    so the writer doesn't have to remember the
    threshold):

      * CV < 0.25 → **MONOTONE** ("drones · break it
        with a short one")
      * 0.25-0.45 → **STEADY** ("workable but can
        sing louder")
      * 0.45-0.80 → **VARIED** ("strong prose rhythm")
      * ≥ 0.80   → **CHOPPY** ("fragments + long
        sentences mixed")

Why CV, not raw stdev?  CV normalises stdev against
the mean, so a 10-word-mean passage with stdev 5 is
correctly rated identically to a 20-word-mean
passage with stdev 10.  Raw stdev would falsely
favour the longer-sentence text.

Verdict-coloured bar chart (one row per sentence) +
three-shortest + three-longest outlier callouts so
the writer sees *which* sentence is at the extreme,
not just that one exists.  Scroll the bar list with
`↑↓` / `PgUp` / `PgDn` / `Home` / `End`; any other
key closes.

Mnemonic: `Shift+H` for *heartbeat* — the felt
rhythm of the prose.

### POV / character chip on the status bar (`Ctrl+B Shift+P`)

The status bar gains a small chip showing the
characters present in the currently-open paragraph,
with the most-mentioned name surfaced as the
heuristic POV character.

Example status line during a third-person limited
chapter from Anna's POV:

```
[Editor]  POV: Anna  +Bob, Carol   • saved 2s ago …
```

Heuristic:

  * The character mentioned most often in the open
    paragraph wins the POV slot.  Rationale: in
    third-person limited prose, the narrator's gaze
    centres on the POV character, so they're
    inherently the most-named entity in the scene.
  * Ties broken by first-mention order.  When two
    characters appear equally often, the one named
    first is usually the scene anchor.
  * Up to three additional named characters trail
    behind as the supporting cast (DIM-styled `+Bob,
    Carol, Dave`) — capped so the chip stays compact
    on narrow terminals.

Wiring: the chip is driven by the project's existing
`characters` lexicon — the paragraphs nested under
the system-tagged Characters book.  No separate
tagging mechanism, no per-paragraph frontmatter, no
POV annotations to maintain.  Add a character to the
project the same way you always did and the chip
starts surfacing them.

Multilingual: the lexicon already runs every name
through every configured Snowball stemmer (English,
Russian, French, German, Spanish), so `Анна` matches
`Анной` / `Анне` / `Анну` and the count is accurate
across the case system.

Config:

```hjson
editor: {
  pov_chip_enabled: true
}
```

Runtime toggle: `Ctrl+B Shift+P` flips the chip on
/ off without rewriting HJSON.  The toggle is
session-local on top of the persisted setting.

First-person POV is a degenerate case (the narrator
is `I`, who isn't in the character lexicon) — for
those scenes the chip correctly surfaces the *other*
prominent character, which is still useful context
("this scene with Bob from Anna's first-person POV").

### Concordance view (`Ctrl+B Shift+L`)

Project-wide concordance: every distinct lexical stem
in the manuscript, ranked by occurrence count, with up
to three KWIC samples per row so the reader can see
*where* a word actually lives in the prose.  Useful for
spotting overworked vocabulary, locating where a
character or place is mentioned, and noticing the
rhythm of repeated lexical motifs.

Pipeline (one-shot at modal open — cached for the
session of the modal):

  1. Walk every `Paragraph` node in the project's
     hierarchy.
  2. Strip the leading `=` heading line so the title
     doesn't inflate body counts.
  3. Tokenise with `unicode-segmentation`'s UAX-#29
     word segmenter — handles Cyrillic, Latin, Greek,
     and Devanagari word boundaries identically.
  4. Drop single-character tokens, pure-digit runs,
     and configured stop-words.  (Stop-words reuse the
     `editor.style_warnings.repeated_phrases.<lang>_
     stop_words` list — same multilingual setup as the
     repeated-phrase detector, no second list to tune.)
  5. Stem each surviving token via the language's
     Snowball algorithm.  `walk`/`walked`/`walking` all
     key on `walk`; Russian `сказал`/`сказала`/
     `сказали` all key on the same stem.  Disable via
     `editor.style_warnings.repeated_phrases.use_stemming
     = false`.
  6. Group by stem-key, count, and capture the first
     three encountered occurrences as KWIC samples
     (32-char half-width, `«match»` wrapping for
     visual contrast in monospace output).
  7. Sort by count descending, ties broken by headword
     ascending.

Modal interactions:

  * Type to filter — case-insensitive substring match
    against the headword *or* any kept variant.  So
    typing `walk` surfaces an entry whose headword is
    `walked` but whose variants include `walking`.
  * `↑` / `↓` / `PgUp` / `PgDn` / `Home` / `End`
    navigate the list.
  * `Ctrl+S` toggles sort mode (count ↔ alphabetical).
    Plain `s` falls through to the filter input so
    headwords beginning with `s` stay typeable.
  * `Esc` closes.

Performance: well under a second on a 100k-word
manuscript; the work runs synchronously on the UI
thread.  Memory cap: max 3 samples + 5 variants per
stem, so even a Tolstoy-scale corpus stays bounded.

Why the same stop-list as `repeated_phrases`?  Both
features want the same answer to "is this word
lexically meaningful?" — and the user already tunes
that list once for the repeated-phrase detector.
Forking a parallel `concordance.stop_words` table
would force authors to keep two lists in sync.

### Scene-break navigation (`Ctrl+B <` / `Ctrl+B >`)

Jump the editor cursor between scene-break lines in
the open paragraph.  Recognised forms are the
typographic dividers writers actually use:

  `* * *`   `***`   `---`   `___`   `###`   `~~~`   `§`

Any line consisting only of 3+ copies of `*`/`-`/`_`/
`~`/`#` (optionally space-separated) counts.  A lone
`§` (section sign) also counts.  Typst headings
(`= Foo`, `== Foo`) deliberately do NOT count — those
are structural section markers, not scene breaks.

Chord rationale: originally requested as
`Ctrl+B Shift+{` / `Ctrl+B Shift+}`.  The `}` half
collides with 1.2.5's `Ctrl+B }` = TagSearch, so the
binding landed on the vim-style `<` / `>` pair —
both free, same ergonomics.  Existing chord muscle
memory preserved.

### Writing-streak heatmap (`Ctrl+B Shift+G`)

GitHub-style 13×7 grid showing the last 91 days of
project-wide word deltas.  Each cell colored by daily
word count bucket — `·` dim gray for 0, `░` faint
green for 1-249, `▒` medium for 250-499, `▓` bright
for 500-999, `█` solid for 1000+.  Today's cell gets
a dark background highlight.

Footer panel reports:
  * current consecutive-writing-days streak
  * longest streak in the 91-day window
  * total words in the window
  * active days × average words/active day
  * legend

Data source is the existing progress store — the same
daily baselines feeding the startup pulse splash and
`Ctrl+V G` modal.  Captured at open time so the
modal is snappy regardless of paragraph count.  Any
key closes.

Streak computation: count consecutive trailing days
with > 0 words.  Today's 0 is a grace (the user might
still be about to write); a 0 yesterday or earlier
breaks the chain.  Longest = maximum run of > 0 days
within the 91-day window.

### TTS save-as-audio (`Ctrl+B Shift+R`)

Companion to the read-aloud chord.  Writes the open
paragraph to an audio file on disk instead of speaking
through the speakers — useful for building draft
"audiobook" previews, sending a chapter to a beta
reader who prefers listening, or just keeping the
prose available for car listening.

The chord opens a path picker pre-filled with
`<project>/audio/<paragraph-slug>.aiff` (slug derived
from the paragraph title; ASCII-only, hyphenated,
falls back to `paragraph` when there's nothing to
slug).  Enter writes, Esc cancels.  Parent directory
auto-creates if missing.

Uses the same voice + speed as `Ctrl+B S` — pulls
them from `editor.tts.voice` / `editor.tts.speed`.
Output format follows the file extension (`.aiff`
default; `.wav` / `.m4a` also work on macOS 13+).
Status bar reports the written file's size + path.

Internally a thin wrapper over `say -o <path>` — the
same subprocess approach that fixed the TTS reuse
bug.  30-second hard cap on the wait so a stuck
subprocess doesn't hang the TUI.

macOS-only in 1.2.9 (`say -o` is macOS-specific).
Non-macOS hosts see the same "TTS is macOS-only"

### Repeated-phrase detector

Second detector under `tui::style_warnings`.  Slides
an `n`-word window across the open paragraph, stems
each window with the project's Snowball algorithm,
and flags every occurrence of any n-gram that repeats
`threshold` or more times.  Hits drawn in soft magenta
+ underlined so they're visually distinct from
filter-word amber.

Catches writer-crutch gestures: `lifted her shoulders`
recurring 3 times in a chapter; `she felt that he`
echoing across paragraphs; `и в этот момент`
appearing in every other scene.

Multilingual via the existing Snowball setup — no new
per-language tuning needed.  `lifted her shoulders`
matches `lifting her shoulders`; `поднял плечи`
matches `подняла плечи` / `подняли плечи`.

Per-language **stop-word lists** filter closed-class
words (`the`, `и`, `der`, …) before n-gram comparison
so common connectives don't inflate counts.  Built-in
defaults ship for each of the five supported
languages; users extend via
`repeated_phrases.<lang>_stop_words`.

Configuration:

```hjson
editor: {
  style_warnings: {
    enabled: true
    repeated_phrases: {
      enabled: true
      n: 4              // window size; 4 is the
                        // editing-craft sweet spot
      threshold: 3      // 3 occurrences = flag
      use_stemming: true
    }
  }
}
```

Toggles with `Ctrl+B Shift+F` alongside the filter-
word overlay.

### Filter-word style overlay

New inline editor overlay flags **filter words** —
the intensifier crutches and hedges that bloat
sentences without adding meaning.  Toggle in-session
via `Ctrl+B Shift+F` (or set
`editor.style_warnings.enabled: true` in HJSON for
default-on).

Multilingual from day one.  Built-in word lists ship
for **English**, **Russian**, **French**, **German**,
**Spanish**.  The active list is keyed by the
project's top-level `language` field.  Russian writers
get a curated list of `очень`, `просто`, `именно`,
`довольно`, `казалось`, `выглядел`, `вдруг`,
`возможно`, and ~25 more — sized to be useful without
being noise.

Flagged spans render in amber + underlined.  Compose
cleanly with existing overlays (selection, search
match, diff-since-save) — the underline persists; the
other styles stack on top.

User extras layer on top of the language default:

```hjson
editor: {
  style_warnings: {
    enabled: true
    filter_words: {
      enabled: true
      extra_words: ["lifted", "shifted", "blinked"]
    }
  }
}
```

Word matching is Unicode-Standard-Annex-#29 compliant
(via `unicode-segmentation`), so Cyrillic / Latin /
Greek / Devanagari word boundaries all work
correctly — no partial-match false positives
(`justice` won't flag because of `just`).  Columns are
char-indexed so multi-byte text doesn't shift the
underline.

This is the first detector under a new
`tui::style_warnings` module — the same infrastructure
will host repeated-phrase / show-don't-tell /
sentence-rhythm detectors as they land.  Each one
slots in as another `StyleWarningKind` variant and
gets its own theme colour.

### Bund word `ink.tts.speak`

Companion to the chord — `( text -- ) ink.tts.speak`
reads the string at the top of the stack aloud through
the same TTS pipeline `Ctrl+B S` uses.  Non-blocking;
subsequent calls interrupt the prior speech.

  bund> "Hello, world" ink.tts.speak
  bund> "Доброе утро" ink.tts.speak

Useful from hooks (`hook.on_save { drop "saved" ink.tts.speak } register`),
from the Ctrl+B E eval modal, or from user scripts in
the Scripts book.  Lives under the new `audio` policy
category — default-allowed.  Bypass-safe: the feature
is still gated by `editor.tts.enabled` in HJSON, so a
script can't produce audio unless the user opted in.

### Paragraph TTS — `Ctrl+B S` reads aloud

`Ctrl+B S` in the editor pane speaks the open
paragraph through the host OS's TTS engine.  Reading
prose aloud catches awkward phrasing that the eye
glosses over; this puts the muscle-memory chord one
keystroke away.

Cross-platform via the **`tts`** crate
(github.com/ndarilek/tts-rs, 20k downloads/90d):

- **macOS** — AVFoundation (the same engine `say`
  wraps).  Russian voices Milena / Yuri / Katya ship
  free with the OS after a one-time language download.
- **Windows** — SAPI / WinRT.  Russian voices Pavel +
  Irina pre-install on Windows 10+.
- **Linux** — Speech Dispatcher.  Requires
  `apt install speech-dispatcher` system-wide; default
  backend (`espeak-ng`) is robotic — config note in
  CONFIGURATION.md points users to RHVoice / piper for
  natural Russian.

Spirit preservation: no new daemons bundled, no paid
service integration, no model downloads inside the
binary.  macOS + Windows are plug-and-play via OS-
shipped voices; Linux needs one `apt install` and
optional voice upgrade.

HJSON config (default off):

```hjson
editor: {
  tts: {
    enabled: false       // master switch
    voice:   "Milena"    // case-insensitive substring match;
                         // picks "(Enhanced)" / "(Premium)"
                         // variant when installed
    speed:   1.0         // multiplier over engine's normal rate
    greeting: ""         // spoken at startup; empty skips
    goodbye:  ""         // spoken at shutdown; empty skips
  }
}
```

**Greeting + goodbye** (1.2.9, added after initial
TTS landing): when set, inkhaven speaks the greeting
at startup (non-blocking, plays in parallel with the
editor coming up after the daily-progress splash) and
the goodbye at shutdown (blocking up to 5 seconds so
the shell doesn't truncate the audio).  Empty
defaults skip both.  Useful for personal welcomes /
sign-offs — `"Welcome back"`, `"Доброе утро,
Владимир"`, etc.

Chord rebind: editor-scope `Ctrl+B S` was previously a
redundant duplicate of plain `Ctrl+S` (Save).
Reclaimed for `editor.tts_read_paragraph`.  Tree-scope
`Ctrl+B S = AddSubchapter` unchanged.

Modal flow:

- **Disabled in HJSON** → friendly "TTS disabled" modal
  with the exact HJSON snippet to enable.
- **Engine init fails** (Linux without speechd, etc.)
  → "TTS unavailable" modal with the engine error +
  per-platform notes.  Failure is cached so we don't
  pay engine-init cost on every Ctrl+B S.
- **Playback in progress** → floating "Read aloud"
  modal with a spinner, elapsed time, chosen voice,
  and the first 80 chars of the paragraph.  Any key
  (Esc / Space / etc.) stops; the modal auto-closes
  when speech ends naturally.

Internals:

- `App.tts_engine: Option<Result<tts::Tts, String>>` —
  lazy-init, cached on both success and failure.
- Main loop polls `tts.is_speaking()` each frame; the
  TtsPlayback modal closes when the engine reports
  idle.  Cheap call (single FFI boolean) so no need to
  gate it behind a tick.
- Leading typst heading line (`= Title`) stripped from
  the spoken text — it's structural, not prose.
- Voice picker preference: substring-match installed
  voices, then pick the candidate that ALSO contains
  "Enhanced" or "Premium" so `voice: "Milena"`
  auto-upgrades to the premium variant when present.
- Rate: `engine.normal_rate() * cfg.speed` clamped to
  the engine's `[min_rate, max_rate]`.  Per-engine
  normalisation so the user thinks in "1.2x normal"
  rather than wpm numbers that vary per platform.

312 tests pass — the new crate is well-tested upstream
and our integration is a single `Tts::default()` call
plus straightforward speak / stop.

# Inkhaven 1.3.0 — Print production (PDF-1)

_The first minor-version milestone since the 1.2 line.  1.2.x built the
deep **middle** of the writing lifecycle — drafting and revising.  1.3
fills the **bookends**: getting a finished manuscript out the door, and
planning a book before the prose exists.  1.3.0 ships the first and
largest piece of that — a complete, self-contained **PDF production
subsystem** for taking a built book all the way to a print shop or a
hand-binding bench._

## The headline — PDF-1, end to end

A reading PDF comes off `inkhaven export pdf` in reading order. That is
the wrong order for a printer, missing a cover, and unchecked for the
problems that only surface in print. 1.3.0 closes every one of those gaps
over a **pure-Rust core** (`lopdf` + `barcoders`) — single binary, **no
external apps** — exposed identically across the CLI (`inkhaven pdf …`),
the `ink.pdf.*` Bund stdlib, and the `Ctrl+B O` book-take pipeline.

### Imposition (the marquee)

`inkhaven pdf impose` reorders a book into folding **signatures** for
hand-binding or a small print shop, and adds the printer marks a binder
needs:

- Binding styles: **perfect-bound**, **saddle-stitch**, **side-stab**.
- **Creep / shingling** — compensates for the inner sheets of a fold
  sticking out, using the paper caliper.
- **Printer marks** — crop, fold, registration, spine stair-step,
  signature number, optional colour bar.
- **Configurable through HJSON** — named profiles in the `imposition:`
  block (`default`, `chapbook` built in; add your own with any
  `sheets_per_signature`, sheet size, orientation, margins, creep, marks).
- `--dry-run` prints the plan (signatures / sheets / creep / first-sheet
  schematic) without writing; **`Ctrl+B Q`** (tree, *Q* for *quire*)
  previews it in the TUI; `imposed_pdf` in `output.extra_formats` imposes
  the just-built book on `Ctrl+B O`.

### Covers, spine, barcode

`inkhaven pdf cover --pages N` generates a one-page cover
`[ bleed | back | spine | front | bleed ]` with the **spine width computed**
from the page count + paper stocks (`cover:` config), optional front art,
back blurb, and a validated **EAN-13 ISBN barcode** (also standalone via
`pdf barcode`). `cover_pdf` is a `Ctrl+B O` book-take.

### Preflight

`inkhaven pdf preflight` catches the print-only problems. The flagship
check is **effective image DPI** — it follows each image through the
page's transformation matrix to find the size it is *actually printed at*,
so a screenshot blown up to fill the page is flagged regardless of what
its file says. Also: font embedding, page-size consistency, blank pages,
colour usage. Profiles (`hand_binding` / `print_shop` / `strict`) set the
DPI target (`preflight:` config).

### Page operations, metadata, outline

The structural toolkit over any PDF: `info`, `extract`, `delete`,
`rotate`, `reorder`, `split`, `merge`, `metadata` (read / set / strip),
`outline` (bookmarks, injected from the book hierarchy on assemble — an
additive, render-inert marker so hand-written `.typ` degrades cleanly).

### Finishing

`grayscale` (desaturates without re-rendering — neutralizes colour
operands + converts RGB/CMYK images to gray), `optimize` (lossless prune +
Flate-compress), `watermark` (translucent text / image stamp over a page
range), `sample` (an evenly-spaced quick-proof subset).

### Surfaces recap

- **CLI** — `inkhaven pdf info|extract|delete|rotate|reorder|split|merge|
  metadata|outline|impose|cover|barcode|preflight|grayscale|optimize|
  watermark|sample`.
- **Bund** — the matching `ink.pdf.*` words (handle-based; only
  `load`/`save` cross disk, gated by the `fs_read`/`fs_write` policy).
- **TUI** — `Ctrl+B Q` imposition preview; `imposed_pdf` / `cover_pdf`
  book-takes.
- **Config** — new `imposition:` / `cover:` / `preflight:` blocks +
  `output.imposed_pdf_config`, all through the project→global cascade.

One new tutorial — [65, Hand-binding](../Tutorials/65-hand-binding.md) —
walks the whole pipeline. Full design + formulas in
[RFC PDF-1](../PROPOSALS/PDF-1.md) and its
[implementation plan](../PROPOSALS/PDF-1_PLAN.md).

### Dependencies

The first runtime dependencies added in several cycles — a deliberate,
audited exception to the standing zero-new-deps stance: **`lopdf`** (pure-
Rust PDF) and **`barcoders`** (EAN-13). Both pure Rust, MIT/Apache, no
external applications; the fidelity of `lopdf` against real typst-pdf
output (fonts / images / vector) was the make-or-break risk and was
cleared with a corpus round-trip gate before anything was built on top.

Tests 1190 → 1270.

_On top of 1.3.0 (Print production / PDF-1).  1.3.0 shipped the **print**

**submission** track: getting a finished manuscript in front of an agent
or editor.  Pure-Rust, no external apps, no new runtime dependencies.

## The Word document agents require

The Shunn manuscript *format* already shipped (`inkhaven manuscript`,
1.2.19) — as typst. But most agents require **Word**. `inkhaven docx`
emits a Shunn-format `.docx`:

```sh
inkhaven docx --book-name "My Novel" --author "Jane Writer" \
    --contact "Jane Writer\n12 Wharf Rd\njane@example.com" --font times
```

Title page (contact corner + rounded word count + centred title/byline),
double-spaced 12 pt Times/Courier, 1″ margins, ½″ first-line indent, a
`Surname / KEYWORD / page` running header from page 2, scene breaks as a
centred `#`, each chapter on a fresh page — reusing the same model as
`manuscript`. **Hand-rolled OOXML** over the in-tree `zip` (the audit
rejected `docx-rs`: it hard-pulls a second major version of `zip` — the
same duplicate-dependency tech debt the lopdf `embed_image` audit
rejected). `docx` is also a `Ctrl+B O` book-take.

## The submission package (AI)

A novel doesn't fit a prompt, so the generators work against a compact
**digest** — title / author / length / a one-line summary of each chapter
+ your Characters and Threads books, cached in `.inkhaven/digest-<slug>.json`
and rebuilt only when the manuscript's structure changes:

```sh
inkhaven submission digest                    # build / refresh the context
inkhaven submission query                     # one-page query letter
inkhaven submission synopsis [--long]         # one-page / 2–3 page, full arc
inkhaven submission comps                     # comp-title suggestions
inkhaven submission logline                   # logline + elevator pitch
```

Each drafts into the new **Submissions** system book (overwriting the same
piece, not piling up) and prints it. Synopses spoil the ending by design;
comp titles are Local-pinned, general-knowledge **suggestions** — labelled
as such, never citing sales figures. From the editor, **`Ctrl+V q`** picks
a generator and streams it into the AI pane; its system prompt resolves
through the usual three tiers (a `submission-*` paragraph in the Prompts
book → `prompts.hjson` → built-in, language-aware), so the house voice is
tunable.

## The tracker

Where it went, when, and what came back — the `.inkhaven/submissions.json`
log, with a **`Ctrl+V u`** modal:

```sh
inkhaven submissions add --market "Dream Literary" --agent "A. Reader" --status sent
inkhaven submissions status S1 offer          # stamps a response date
inkhaven submissions add-note S1 "got a call — requested first 50 pages"
inkhaven submissions list [--json|--status sent|--open]
```

`add-note` is a **timestamped event trail**, so a record reads as a
history (sent → requested edits → round two). In the modal, `↑↓` move,
`Space`/`s` cycle status, `d` removes; the selected record expands to show
its trail. Link a generated draft with `--draft <slug>`.

## Scripting (Bund)

Five `ink.export.*` words — `docx | manuscript | markdown | tex | epub`,
each `( book path -- )` — so a release script emits every prose artefact in
one pass, alongside the `ink.pdf.*` print pipeline. All `fs_write`-gated
and path-sandboxed like every disk-crossing `ink.*` word.

# Inkhaven 1.3.10 — Semantic drift

_On top of 1.3.8's world-consistency tools. 1.3.8 caught **hard**
contradictions — a fact clashing with a fact. 1.3.10 catches **soft** drift:
two descriptions of the same entity that diverge across the manuscript without
a clean factual clash — a tavern "cramped and smoky" in ch.2, "airy and
bright" in ch.20. It's also the bridge to the 1.4 Whole-Book AI Editor: it
builds and proves the retrieve-then-reason loop. Full plan:
[WORLD-2_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-2_PLAN.md)._

## The honest design: embeddings retrieve, the AI adjudicates

Neither half works alone. Cosine similarity finds same-topic descriptions but
can't tell contradiction from relatedness ("cramped and smoky" and "airy and
bright" are highly *similar* yet opposite). An antonym lexicon is hopelessly
brittle. So drift splits the work: **embeddings retrieve** the handful of
paragraphs that describe an entity, and an **AI pass adjudicates** which
contradict.

Crucially, it **reuses the vector index that's already built as you write** —
every paragraph is embedded on save (the same index `Ctrl+F` searches). No new
indexing step, no bulk re-embed.

## `inkhaven drift scan`

For each Character, Place, and Artefact, Inkhaven retrieves the paragraphs that
describe it (keeping only the ones that actually *name* it — the anchor that
drops topical false-positives), then asks the model which descriptions
contradict:

```
drift scan: 1 description contradiction(s):
  ⚠ The Drunken Goose (place) — [ch.2] “cramped and smoky”  ⟷  [ch.20] “airy and bright”
      ↳ the same tavern can't be both without a renovation the story never shows
```

Cached in `.inkhaven/drift.json` (order-independent content hash), `--json` for
a CI gate. `inkhaven drift list` previews the retrieved descriptions
deterministically, no AI.

## In the Editorial Pass

Drift contradictions surface in `inkhaven edit` and the `Ctrl+V Shift+R`
cockpit as the `drift` category (Warn), ranked with everything else and
**jump-only** — `Enter` lands on the *later*, divergent passage. There's no
honest single-paragraph rewrite for "the atmosphere changed across 18
chapters"; you reconcile the two passages. `inkhaven edit --deep` now runs the
drift scan alongside the facts / tension / continuity ones.

## In the story bible

`Ctrl+V Shift+L` becomes a continuity-at-a-glance view: under any flagged
entity, a **⚠ drift** badge (amber) names the contradicting descriptions, the
model's reason, and the entity's full chapter-ordered **description trail** —
every passage that described it, in order, each a jump to its source. The scan
persists the trail in the sidecar, so the bible renders it with no embedding
load in the TUI.

## Tuning

```hjson
drift: {
  top_k: 24          // vector hits pulled per entity before name-filtering
  max_snippets: 8    // descriptions kept per entity (bounds the judge prompt)
}
```

## Under the hood

- Zero new dependencies (fastembed + genai were already in the tree). The
  retrieval reuses the on-save vector index; the judge mirrors the
  `facts check` AI-pass + content-hashed sidecar pattern.
- New pure, unit-tested code in `src/drift.rs`: `assemble_descriptions` (name
  anchor + dedup + chapter order + cap), `parse_drift_pairs`,
  `resolve_conflicts`, the `DriftReport` round-trip.
- Honest limits, stated in the tutorial: retrieval-bounded (misses
  pronoun-only description), AI-judged (needs a provider), needs the index
  populated.
- Tests 1339 → 1346. New tutorial 70; quick-help + the `Ctrl+V Shift+L`
  description refreshed.

_Rounds out the world-consistency pillar (1.3.8 hard facts, 1.3.10 soft

Full plan: [WORLD-3_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-3_PLAN.md)._

## Drift reads pronouns now (and in five languages)

The 1.3.10 retriever kept only paragraphs that *named* the entity, missing
the commonest description shape — "Mara crossed the yard. **She** was taller…"
1.3.11 adds **coreference-lite**: walking each chapter, it tracks the most
recently, *unambiguously* named entity per kind and attributes a name-less,
pronoun-carrying paragraph to it. Two same-kind names clear the anchor (no
guessing); attribution never crosses a chapter — precision-favouring, with the
AI judge as the backstop.

It's **multilingual**: built-in pronoun sets ship for English, Russian,
French, German, and Spanish, keyed by the project `language` (so "Она была
выше" attributes in Russian exactly as "She was taller" does in English).
Articles and high-frequency homographs are excluded; the `mentions`
word-boundary check is Unicode-aware (so "Мара" / "José" don't mis-match
mid-word). Nothing to configure — re-run `drift scan`.

## `inkhaven world` — the consistency snapshot

```sh
inkhaven world            # the dashboard
inkhaven world --json     # CI gate
inkhaven world --deep     # refresh facts-check / facts-scan / drift / continuity first
inkhaven world --entity Mara   # zoom to one entity
```

A sectioned snapshot — a health line (`World: 2 issue(s) — 1 fact conflict ·
1 drift`), then Facts (established / internal conflicts / prose contradictions),
Drift, Continuity, Anachronisms, and Coverage. It **complements** `inkhaven
edit`: `edit` is a walkable worklist of everything; `world` is a focused
*snapshot* of the world layer, grouped by fact and entity. The same one-line
summary now banners the top of the `Ctrl+V Shift+L` story bible.

## Coverage: the dangling cast

`world` (and `inkhaven edit`, as an `info` `coverage` finding) flags entities
defined in the Characters / Places / Artefacts books but **never named in the
prose** — a character you sketched but never wrote in. The `edit` finding jumps
to the entity's bible definition. Silent on an unwritten draft.

## Smaller niceties

- **Anachronisms, named** — `world` lists each flagged term + its chapter, not
  just a count.
- **`--entity` drilldown** — `world --entity <name>` shows one entity's drift,
  description trail, tracked attributes, and prose-named status; `drift list
  --entity <name>` scopes the retrieval preview.

## Under the hood

- Zero new dependencies. Drift depth is pure heuristics; the world report
  aggregates existing sidecars + cheap counts.
- New pure, unit-tested code: `drift::attribute_continuations` /
  `pronouns` (per-language) / `mentions` (Unicode boundary), and
  `world_report` (`issue_count` / `summary` / `undescribed_of`).

# Inkhaven 1.3.12 — The background deep refresh

_The world-consistency checks (facts, drift, continuity) are AI passes — a
multi-minute batch. Until now you ran them from the CLI and waited. 1.3.12
brings the whole batch inside the editor, on a background thread, so you never
leave your prose and never freeze the UI. Full plan:
[DEEP-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/DEEP-1_PLAN.md)._

## `Ctrl+V Shift+F` — refresh in the background

One chord runs `facts check` + `facts scan` + `drift scan` + `continuity
extract` (the `inkhaven world --deep` set, **in the manuscript's language**)
on a background thread. A **`⟳ deep refresh`** chip in the status bar tracks
progress; the editor stays fully responsive — keep writing. When it finishes,
an open story bible (`Ctrl+V Shift+L`) or Editorial Pass (`Ctrl+V Shift+R`)
**rebuilds itself** from the fresh findings and the status shows the new
`inkhaven world` summary. One refresh at a time; needs an LLM provider.

## It's advisory — it never edits your text

The deep refresh **reads** your manuscript and **writes findings** to
`.inkhaven/*.json` sidecars. It does not change a word of your prose — no
paragraphs created, edited, or deleted. The only thing that ever rewrites
prose is the Editorial Pass's `f` / `F`, always user-initiated, snapshotted,
and shown as a diff to accept or reject. The background refresh never touches
that path.

## Stale findings announce themselves

Findings live in their sidecars until you re-run a scan, so a finding can
predate a fix. Each scan now stamps a cheap fingerprint of the manuscript
(every paragraph's `(id, modified_at)` — no content reads); when the prose has
moved since, the world report, the bible banner, and the Editorial Pass show
**`⚠ may be stale`** with a nudge to re-run. It only *warns* — never hides or
deletes a finding.

## How it can run while you write

DuckDB is single-writer, so a second process can't open the project the TUI
holds. Instead the refresh runs in-process on a thread that **shares** a clone
of the editor's connection pool — no second open, no lock. The pool (4
connections by default) is now tunable via **`embeddings.pool_size`** (clamped
to ≥2 so the background read and your foreground edits never contend). Quitting
mid-refresh simply abandons the run: finished sidecars are valid (atomic
writes), an unfinished one is merely stale, never corrupt.

## Under the hood

- Zero new dependencies (`std::thread` + `std::sync::mpsc`; r2d2 already in).
- A reusable **background-job harness** (`start_bg_job` / `pump_bg_job` /
  `BgMsg`) the 1.4 Whole-Book AI Editor will reuse for retrieve-then-reason
  queries.
- The four world-layer scans gained store-injected `*_with` variants (the CLI
  commands are unchanged thin wrappers); `deep_refresh_shared` orchestrates
  them against the shared store, threading `cfg.language` so the deep AI runs
  in the manuscript's language.
- New pure, unit-tested code: `drain_bg_messages`, `world_report::
  manuscript_fingerprint` / `is_stale`.
- Tests 1354 → 1359. New tutorial 72.

## Carryovers (still open)

- **The Whole-Book AI Editor** (general retrieve-then-reason) — the 1.4
  headline; it reuses the background-job harness.
- Cancelling an in-flight job (vs abandon-on-quit); a multi-job queue.
- PDF N-up / booklet presets; CMYK-JPEG grayscale; ePub inline images + popup
  footnotes; sixth supported language.

# Inkhaven 1.3.13 — Breadth: every language, cancellable jobs, print & ebook polish _1.3.8–1.3.12 went **deep** on the world layer (facts, drift, continuity, the background refresh). 1.3.13 goes **wide**: it makes the AI/NLP features work in **any** language — not just the five with hand-curated word lists — lets you **cancel** a long background job mid-flight, and finishes the **print** and **ebook** export paths. Full plan: [BREADTH-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/BREADTH-1_PLAN.md). Zero new dependencies._ ## Cancel a deep refresh in flight The background deep refresh (1.3.12) is a multi-minute AI batch. Until now, once you pressed `Ctrl+V Shift+F` you waited for the whole thing — four scans — or quit. Now **re-pressing `Ctrl+V Shift+F` while it runs cancels it**: the status chip shows `⟳ deep refresh · cancelling…`, each scan checks a shared cancel flag between chapters/entities and stops at the next boundary, and whatever finished still wrote its sidecars (the completion reports `cancelled` rather than `done`). The cancel flag threads all the way down — `facts scan`, `drift scan`, and `continuity extract` each take a `cancel: &AtomicBool` and honour it per unit of work — so a cancel lands in seconds, not at the end of the current scan. ## Full multilingual — it works in your language, or it tells you it doesn't Inkhaven's style + world tooling has always been keyed to the project `language`. But "keyed to" used to mean **five** languages with curated word lists (en/ru/fr/de/es), and an **honesty bug**: an uncurated language silently fell back to the *English* lists, so a Polish or Japanese project got English filter-words flagged in its prose. 1.3.13 fixes the honesty and removes the five-language ceiling. ### Honest fallback — no more English masquerade The built-in detector lists (filter words, show-don't-tell, repeated-phrase stop-words, drift pronouns) now return **empty** for a language with no curated list, never English. An uncurated language gets *no* false flags rather than wrong-language ones. Stemming (Snowball, 18 languages) and the multilingual embedding model already worked for far more than five languages; this aligns the word-list layer with that honesty. ### `inkhaven lang status` — an honest coverage matrix ``` inkhaven lang status [--language ] ``` prints exactly what's automatic, curated, or off for your project (or any `--language`): stemming, filter words, show-don't-tell, stop-words, drift pronouns, anachronism lexicon, embeddings, AI world-check **output language**, and AI world-check **prompts** — each marked `✓` / `built-in N` / `none`. When nothing is curated, it points you at `lang bootstrap`. ### `inkhaven lang bootstrap ` — curate any language with one command ``` inkhaven lang bootstrap polish [--provider

] [--yes] ``` asks your LLM (as a careful lexicographer, output forced to the requested language, lemma forms for Snowball) for the full detector vocabulary — filter words, the four show-don't-tell categories, stop-words, and the three pronoun sets — and prints it as a ready-to-paste HJSON snippet. `--yes` patches `inkhaven.hjson` in place (versioned backup + atomic write + comment preservation). This is the bridge from "five languages" to "any language": bootstrap once, verify with `lang status`, tune by hand. ### World-check prompts speak your language All four world-consistency scans — facts **check** (internal fact contradictions), facts **scan** (prose-vs-fact), **drift**, **continuity** — now run with system prompts **localized** to the project language (en/ru/fr/de/es built in), and force their findings' explanations to be written **in that language**. An uncurated language falls back to the English prompt **with a warning** (never silently). Each prompt is overridable through a **3-tier cascade**: a `Prompts` book entry (`{slug}-{lang}` → `{slug}`) → `prompts.hjson` → the localized built-in. The fact-check prompt also reasons about world domains (planetary science, physics, geology, hydrology, climate, ecology), treating your invented rules as authoritative — so it catches *internal* contradictions ("winters are mild" ⟷ "the harbor freezes each January"), not just textual ones. ### Per-language config, not five fixed fields The detector config moved from five fixed per-language fields to **maps** keyed by language name, so a config can populate *any* language: ``` editor: { style_warnings: { filter_words: { languages: { polish: [ … ] } } show_dont_tell: { languages: { polish: { linking_verbs: […], emotion_adjectives: […], … } } } repeated_phrases:{ languages: { polish: [ …stop-words… ] } } } } drift: { pronouns: { polish: { character: […], place: […], artefact: […] } } } ``` Two worked examples ship in [`custom_languages/`](../../custom_languages/) — **Arabic** (RTL, pro-drop, suffix pronouns) and **Hungarian** (agglutinative, genderless 3rd person) — alongside a README. ## Print: a one-command booklet and a proper A5 codex The 1.3.0 imposition engine (`inkhaven pdf impose`) already plans saddle-stitch and perfect-bound signatures from named profiles. 1.3.13 adds the two recipes home binders reach for most. ### `inkhaven pdf booklet` — zero-config saddle stitch ``` inkhaven pdf booklet book.pdf # auto-fit the sheet to 2× the page inkhaven pdf booklet book.pdf --sheet A3 # …or centre the spread on a preset ``` No profile, no config file. The press sheet **auto-fits to two source pages side-by-side**, so *any* trim size works — not just the preset-bound `chapbook` profile. All pages nest into one folded signature; blanks balance around the centre fold. `--creep` adds shingle compensation for thick booklets, `--no-marks` gives a clean already-trimmed proof, `--dry-run` previews the plan. ### `a5_book` profile — a real A5 book from A4 sheets ``` inkhaven pdf impose book.pdf --config a5_book ``` The popular home-binding recipe: a proper **A5 codex** folded from A4 sheets. **Perfect-bound** (gathered + glued/sewn signatures) rather than saddle-stitched, so it scales to a full-length book where the saddle path tops out around 40 pages. Four A4 sheets per signature = 16 A5 pages (the standard home section), shingle creep keeps the fold square, and the **signature-number mark** lets you gather sections in order by hand. (Source pages should already be A5 trim — imposition centres, it doesn't scale.) ## Ebook: inline images and popup footnotes in the EPUB The EPUB export (`inkhaven epub`) gained the two pieces it was missing. - **Inline images** — `Image` nodes in a chapter, previously dropped, now embed as EPUB3 `

# Inkhaven 1.3.14 — The ConLang Suite (Part 1: phonology, lexicon, morphology)

_Inkhaven becomes the first constructed-language workbench that lives **inside
the writing tool**. A fantasy or sci-fi author can now build a language —
phonology, lexicon, morphology — and write prose in it, with the AI as an
assistant and the author in full deterministic control of the rules. This is
the first checkpoint of a flagship that continues across 1.3.x (RFC LANG-1;
plan: [LANG-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/LANG-1_PLAN.md)). Zero new dependencies._

The suite is layered **on top of the existing 1.2.13 `Language` system book** —
the book stays the home of record, and these engines reconstruct an in-memory
model from its HJSON chapters. Reference: [CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md).

## The phonology engine (P1)

A complete, deterministic sound system — inventory through tone:

- **Inventory + phonotactics** — phonemes (IPA + romanization), named classes,
  syllable templates, and a phonotactic validator (`max_cluster_size`,
  `no_geminate`, `forbid_bigram`, and — syllable-aware — `forbid_in_onset` /
  `forbid_in_coda` / `sonority_sequencing`). A **deterministic word generator**
  samples templates and keeps only words that satisfy every constraint:
  `inkhaven language generate-word`.
- **Syllabification** — sonority-peak nuclei + the Maximal Onset Principle:
  `inkhaven language syllabify` (`star.ka`, `al.tan`).
- **Allophony** — ordered SPE-style rules (`k > tʃ / _ i`, `d > t / _ #`,
  `∅ > ə / C _ C`) derive the surface form from the underlying:
  `inkhaven language ipa`.
- **Stress** — fixed (initial / final / penult / antepenult) or the
  weight-sensitive Latin rule: `inkhaven language stress` (`ta.ˈki.na`).
- **Romanization** — named, **bidirectional** schemes with contextual rules
  that disambiguate shared graphemes (`c` → /s/ before a front vowel, else
  /k/): `inkhaven language romanize [--reverse] [--scheme]`.
- **Tone** — register / contour systems with sandhi (Mandarin `3 3 → 2 3`):
  `inkhaven language tone --tones "…"`.

## The lexicon + AI dictionary generation (P2)

- **AI dictionary generation** with a **complete dedup gate** —
  `inkhaven language generate-lexicon --topic … --count …`. The forms come
  from the deterministic generator (so every proposal obeys the phonotactics);
  the AI assigns meanings, glossed **in your working language**. The gate
  rejects any proposal that is illegal, a **homophone** of an existing word, a
  **duplicate meaning**, or — with `--semantic` — a **near-synonym** (embedding
  cosine, so "stone" vs "rock" is caught). Nothing commits without `--yes`;
  generated entries are tagged with register + semantic domain.
- **Audit** — `inkhaven language audit` flags phonotactic violations,
  homophones, and duplicate meanings across the whole dictionary.
- **Rich entries + query** — entries carry register / domain / era / etymology
  tags; `inkhaven language query [--register] [--domain] [--era] [--pos]
  [--text]` filters by any combination.
- **Worldbuilding links** — `inkhaven language link-place` / `link-character`
  (proficiency) / `speakers`, stored in a `.inkhaven/conlang-links.json`
  sidecar (the prose Places/Characters books are never touched).
- **Manuscript scan** — `inkhaven language scan-manuscript` finds candidate
  *undefined* conlang words in your prose (words that look like the language
  but aren't in the dictionary).

## Morphology (P3, started)

- **Paradigm generation** — `inkhaven language paradigm --root … --template …`
  applies a paradigm template's morpheme sequence to a root and runs the
  allophony engine **across the affix boundaries**, emitting the surface form +
  a Leipzig gloss. So `kata` + DAT → `katat` (final devoicing), while `kata` +
  DAT + PL → `katadi` (the now-medial `d` correctly stays). The morphology
  HJSON lives in the **Grammar** chapter.

## In the editor

- **`Ctrl+B X` — the ConLang hub.** A read-only overview of every language:
  phoneme inventory, template / constraint / allophony counts, prosody,
  romanization schemes, lexicon size, and linked speakers.
- **`:lang:` inline insertion.** Type `:<language>:` (by name or ISO code) in
  the editor and a filterable lexicon picker inserts the chosen word in place
  of the trigger. (`Ctrl+B Q` translation, from 1.2.13, is unchanged.)

## Design notes

- **Forms obey the language; meanings come from the AI; nothing duplicates.**
  The deterministic generator is the single source of word *forms*; the AI only
  chooses among valid forms and assigns *meaning*; every AI proposal passes the
  dedup gate. AI features are advisory — proposal-gated, `--yes`-committed,
  glosses in the project working language.
- **Extend in place.** No parallel "Languages" book, no schema migration — the
  morphology block lives in the Grammar chapter, the phonology block in the
  Phonology chapter, the lexicon stays the existing `DictionaryEntry`
  paragraphs. The one normalized concession (per-gloss embeddings) is computed
  on demand, reusing the store's already-loaded model.
- **Pure + tested.** Every deterministic engine (validator, syllabifier,
  allophony, stress, romanization round-trip, tone sandhi, paradigm generation,
  the dedup gate) is unit/property-tested; the AI calls are thin layers.

## What's next (still in flight)

LANG-1 continues across 1.3.x: more morphology (auto-gloss, the grammar
questionnaire, derived forms), **diachronics** (sound-change engine, cognates,
family trees), **writing systems + pure-Rust font compilation** (the one
dep-heavy phase), an **analysis suite**, and a package-rich **Typst grammar
book / dictionary** export.

Tests 1359 (1.3.13) → 1428. Zero new dependencies. The whole surface is
documented in [CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md).

# Inkhaven 1.3.15 — The ConLang Suite (Part 2: morphology & diachronics)

_1.3.14 shipped the ConLang substrate — phonology, lexicon, and the start of
morphology. 1.3.15 builds two whole pillars on top of it: the rest of
**morphology** (paradigms ↔ glossing ↔ derivation ↔ grammar ↔ expressions) and
all of **diachronics** (how a language changes over time and spawns daughter
languages). RFC LANG-1; reference [CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md). Zero new
dependencies._

A through-line of this release: **everything reuses the engines already built.**
The auto-glosser generates paradigms forward to dodge reverse-parsing; the
sound-change engine *is* the allophony rewrite engine; derivation and cognates
share the affix-application path. One deterministic core, many surfaces.

## Morphology, completed (P3)

- **Auto-gloss** — `inkhaven language gloss <lang> --text "kata katai katat"`
  prints an aligned Leipzig interlinear. It recognises inflected *and*
  allophony-altered forms (`katat` → `stone-DAT`) by generating each entry's
  paradigm forward and matching — so the allophony is handled, not fought.
  Entries opt in with a `paradigm:` field.
- **Derived-form proposals** — `inkhaven language derive --root kata --pos verb`
  coins *new lexemes* (agent nouns, diminutives, …) via derivational rules,
  with allophony; advisory (`--yes` commits, recording the etymology).
- **Grammar questionnaire** — `inkhaven language grammar <lang>` walks a
  WALS-aligned catalog of 16 typological features (word order, alignment, case,
  tense/aspect/mood, negation, …); `--set word_order=sov` validates the answer
  against the catalog.
- **Idioms & metaphors** — `inkhaven language idiom-add` / `metaphor-add` /
  `idioms` store phrase-level expressions the AI translation consults to stay
  idiomatic.

## Diachronics (P4)

- **Sound-change engine** — a sound change *is* an ordered context rewrite, so
  the engine reuses the allophony rewrite engine. `inkhaven language
  sound-change <lang> --form tap` → `taf`; a `{ diachronics: { proto, rules } }`
  block in the Phonology chapter declares the chain.
- **Daughter-language derivation** — `inkhaven language derive-lexicon
  <daughter> [--yes]` evolves a proto's *whole dictionary* through the
  daughter's chain, carrying glosses forward and recording each etymology.
- **Cognate sets + family tree** — `inkhaven language family-tree` draws the
  genealogical tree; `inkhaven language cognates ProtoEldarin --form takap`
  traces a proto-form's reflex in every daughter (`Eldar takaf` vs `Sindarin
  tahaf`).
- **AI comparative reconstruction + realism check** — `inkhaven language
  reconstruct --forms "tava taba"` proposes a proto-form from cognates;
  `inkhaven language realism-check <lang>` assesses whether the sound-change
  chain is typologically plausible. Advisory.

## Design notes

- **Deterministic where it can be.** Every engine here — paradigm generation,
  auto-gloss, derivation, the sound-change chain, cognate reflexes, the family
  tree, the grammar catalog — is a pure, unit/property-tested function. Only the
  reconstruction + realism checks (and translation) call the LLM, as thin
  layers.
- **Extend in place.** No new chapters: morphology + grammar + idioms blocks
  live in the existing **Grammar** chapter, diachronics in **Phonology**, the
  lexicon stays the existing dictionary paragraphs. A shared
  `upsert_grammar_paragraph` writes the structured blocks.
- **AI stays advisory** — proposals (`--yes`-committed), glosses + reasoning in
  the project working language.

## What's next

The remaining LANG-1 pillars: **writing systems + pure-Rust font compilation**
(the one dependency-heavy phase — fontc / norad / etc.), an **analysis suite**,
and a package-rich **Typst grammar book / dictionary** export. Then polish.

Tests 1428 (1.3.14) → 1439. Zero new dependencies. Full surface:
[CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md).

# Inkhaven 1.3.16 — The ConLang Suite (Part 3: writing systems, fonts & output)

_1.3.14–1.3.15 built the spoken language — phonology, lexicon, morphology,
diachronics. 1.3.16 builds the **written** one: a constructed script goes from
hand artwork or an AI description all the way to a real TrueType font, a Typst
layout, and a typed input method — and the language starts becoming a **book**.
RFC LANG-1; reference [CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md)._

This is the one dependency-heavy phase the plan always flagged. It adds **one
new crate** — `norad` (a pure-Rust UFO reader/writer) — for the fonts pillar the
user approved. The in-process TrueType compiler reuses `write-fonts` + `kurbo`,
which were **already in the dependency tree** (via `typst` / `krilla`), so they
add no new compiled crate; `fontc` was deliberately *not* used (it would have
dragged in `fontir` / `fontbe` plus a duplicate `write-fonts`). `skrifa` is a
test-only dev-dependency, also already in the tree.

## Writing systems + fonts (P5)

A complete pipeline from glyph to font, fully in-process — no external tool:

- **Glyph suitability preflight** — `language glyph-lint --svg a.svg` checks an
  SVG is fit for a font outline (filled paths required; stroke-only / raster /
  gradient artwork is flagged). It also catches the **counter mistake**: a
  near-white fill among darker ones is almost always a hole the author drew with
  white paint, which a monochrome font won't honour.
- **SVG → UFO** — `language font-build` compiles a directory of glyph SVGs into
  a UFO font source (via `norad`).
- **UFO → TrueType, in-process** — `--format ttf|both` assembles a complete
  OpenType table set (`glyf`/`loca`/`cmap`/`head`/`hhea`/`maxp`/`hmtx`/`name`/
  `post`/`OS-2`) directly with `write-fonts`; cubics are quadified for the
  `glyf` table. The result opens in any font tool and passes a fontTools
  structural round-trip.
- **Config-driven font block + binding** — `language font-import-glyph` binds a
  glyph to a phoneme and a Unicode codepoint, stores the artwork, and records it
  in a `font` block in the language; `font-config` lists the bindings;
  `font-build --language <lang>` compiles the script straight from the book.
- **AI text-to-SVG glyph draft** — `language glyph-draft --describe "…"` has the
  model draft an SVG glyph, run through the same preflight, advisory (`--yes`
  binds a usable draft). The prompt instructs the model to cut counters with
  **reverse-wound subpaths**, not white fills. _Validated live against DeepSeek:
  drafting, preflight, binding, and compilation all produce a renderable font._
- **Spatial templates — composed blocks & layout** — one `SpatialTemplate`
  engine, two binding times. `language font-compose` bakes component glyphs into
  one precomposed block (a Hangul-style syllable square, an Egyptian quadrat);
  `language spatial-typst` arranges them at **layout time** in a Typst quadrat
  (the hieroglyphic path — no combinatorial precomposition). Built-in templates
  `lr` / `tb` / `quad` / `stack3`, or define your own.
- **Input method** — `language transliterate --text "katha"` types the script:
  romanized input → glyph codepoints via the font bindings, longest key first so
  a digraph (`th`, `ka`) beats its prefixes.

## Analysis (P6.1)

- **`language stats <lang>`** — a descriptive profile (vs `audit`, which hunts
  for problems): inventory balance (consonants / vowels), phoneme frequency
  across the lexicon, the syllable-length distribution (with bars), which onsets
  and codas get used, and the part-of-speech spread.

## Dictionary output (P6.2)

- **`language dictionary <lang> --format md|typ`** — render the lexicon as a
  real document. Markdown is a clean alphabetized listing; **Typst is the
  showpiece**: a paginated, two-column A5 book with a title page and overview
  table that — when the language has a `font` block — shows each headword in the
  **native script** (transliterated by the input method) beside its
  romanization, pronunciation, POS, and gloss. Compiles to a PDF that embeds and
  renders the conscript font.

## Design notes

- **Deterministic core, thin AI layer.** Every engine — the preflight, the
  SVG→UFO→TTF compiler, the spatial composition, the input method, the analysis
  profile, the document renderers — is a pure, unit-tested function. Only the
  glyph drafter calls the LLM, as a thin layer behind the preflight.
- **AI stays advisory** — the glyph draft is proposal-gated (`--yes`-committed),
  validated through the suitability preflight before it can be bound.
- **Reuse over new deps.** The TrueType compiler builds on crates already in the
  tree; only `norad` is genuinely new, for the approved fonts pillar.
