# Inkhaven 1.3.18 — The ConLang Suite: morphology depth & a developer's guide

_With RFC LANG-1 complete (1.3.17), this release deepens the one area that still
had a clear functional ceiling — **morphology** — and ships a complete,
beginner-friendly **book** about the whole suite. No new dependencies. Reference:
[CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md)._

## Morphology depth

Until now a word changed shape only by gluing prefixes and suffixes to its edges.
1.3.18 adds the rest of how the world's languages actually mark grammar.

- **Non-concatenative morphology.** A morpheme can now be an **infix** (inserted
  inside the root — `sulat` → `s-um-ulat`, anchored before or after the first
  vowel), a **circumfix** (wrapping the root — `form: "ge_t"` → *ge* + stem +
  *t*), an **ablaut** process (`process: "ablaut"` with SPE `rules`, swapping a
  sound inside the stem — `sing` → `sang`), or **reduplication**
  (`process: "reduplication"`, mode `full` / `initial_cv` / `initial_syllable` /
  `final_syllable` — `kata` → `kakata`). All are written as ordinary morphemes
  and used in paradigm cells just like affixes, with allophony applying across
  every new seam.

- **Affix precedence.** An optional `precedence` on a morpheme controls how close
  it sits to the root when several stack (`0` = any, `1` = root-adjacent, `2` =
  the next slot out, …) — so the case suffix can always hug the root and the
  number suffix sit outside it, regardless of the order a cell lists them.

- **Agreement (concord).** A new `agreement` block declares that a dependent part
  of speech copies grammatical features from its head — an adjective agreeing
  with its noun, a verb with its subject. **`inkhaven language agree <lang>
  --word mira --pos adjective --features "number=pl"`** inflects the dependent to
  match (`mira` → `mirai`, glossed `bright-PL`).

## A reference grammar that groups by category

The grammar book now reads each morpheme's `category` and `value` (case, number,
tense, …) and groups affixes by category, showing each one's kind (prefix /
suffix / infix / circumfix / ablaut / reduplication) and value — instead of a
flat list. Agreement rules get their own section, and the AI study guide and
tutorial explain the new processes when a language uses them.

## A developer's guide: *Developing a Constructed Language with Inkhaven*

A new ~120-page book, [`Book/CONLANG_DEVELOPMENT/`](../../Book/CONLANG_DEVELOPMENT/),
teaches the entire ConLang Suite from zero — for a reader who knows neither
linguistics nor Inkhaven. Every linguistic term is defined where it first
appears; the book starts from installing the tool and walks the whole process
(phonology → lexicon → grammar → diachronics → writing systems → producing the
books) one pillar at a time, ending with a complete worked walkthrough. It is
typeset in the *Book of Inkhaven* style and compiles with a bare `typst compile`.
A full command reference, a configuration-block reference, and a glossary of
every term are included as appendices.

## Design notes

- **Backward compatible.** Existing paradigms behave identically — `precedence`
  defaults to "any", and the new affix types and processes are opt-in.
- **Deterministic core.** Infix / circumfix / ablaut / reduplication, precedence
  ordering, and agreement are all pure, unit-tested functions; ablaut reuses the
  allophony rewrite engine and agreement reuses paradigm generation.

Tests 1490 → 1498. **Zero new dependencies.** Full reference:

# Inkhaven 1.3.19 — The ConLang Suite: syntax, interchange & creative text

_RFC LANG-1 was complete at 1.3.17; 1.3.18 deepened morphology. 1.3.19 makes a
constructed language **speak** — a real syntax engine that assembles whole
sentences and the constructions built on them — and lets it **travel**:
interchange with other conlang tools, a coverage gauge, and creative-text
generators. No new dependencies. Reference: [CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md)._

## Speaking the language: the syntax engine

Until now Inkhaven inflected single words. 1.3.19 assembles them into clauses and
builds the constructions a grammar needs.

- **Sentences.** **`inkhaven language sentence`** takes a subject, verb, and
  object (each `root` or `root:gloss`, with optional adjective and number) and
  builds the clause: it *orders* the constituents by your `word_order`, *assigns
  case* by your `alignment` (nominative–accusative or ergative–absolutive),
  *inflects* each noun through the `noun` paradigm, and *runs agreement* (the
  adjective takes its noun's case, the verb agrees with its subject). The output
  is the surface clause, an interlinear gloss, and a literal. The **grammar book**
  now prints a worked example sentence drawn from your own lexicon.

- **Negation & polar questions.** `sentence --negate [--negator W]` and
  `--question [--q-particle W]` realize negation and yes/no questions per your
  `negation` and `question` typology features — a particle/auxiliary before the
  verb or an affix fused onto it; a question particle, verb inversion, or verb
  morphology. With no word supplied, only the gloss is marked — never an invented
  form.

- **Relative clauses.** **`inkhaven language relative`** builds a noun modified by
  a relative clause ("the bird that sees the stone"). The head plays a role
  inside the embedded clause — its subject or object, the *gap* — and the embedded
  clause runs through the same engine, so it case-marks and agrees correctly.
  Placement (prenominal vs postnominal) follows your `relative_clause` feature.

- **Coordination.** **`inkhaven language coordinate`** joins two or more noun
  phrases (`--np`) or whole clauses (`--clause`) with a conjunction — "bird and
  stone", "bird sees stone and river falls" — each clause assembled in full.

Every construction reads from the same typology answers and paradigms as a plain
sentence, so the richer sentences cost nothing once the grammar is in place.

## Letting the language travel: interchange

- **Broader exporters.** `language export --format` gains **`xliff`** (an XLIFF
  1.2 translation memory loadable in OmegaT / memoQ / Weblate), **`linguex`**
  (LaTeX for the `linguex` package — glossed headwords + numbered examples), and
  **`ipa-chart`** (a Markdown inventory), alongside the existing json / anki / csv.

- **Importers beyond own-CSV.** **`inkhaven language import --format`** reads
  **`toolbox`** (Toolbox / MDF Standard Format — the same SFM that SIL Toolbox,
  FieldWorks, and **Lexique Pro** use) and **`polyglot`** (a PolyGlot dictionary —
  the native `.pgd` archive is unzipped automatically, or a raw `.xml`). Import
  **previews by default** and writes nothing until `--yes`.

## Filling the gaps, and having fun

- **Semantic-gap finder.** **`inkhaven language gaps`** diffs your lexicon against
  a reference concept scope — the bundled **Swadesh-100** (translated into every
  working language) or your own HJSON topic list — and reports the missing
  concepts, frequency-ranked, shaped to hand straight to `generate-lexicon`.

- **Creative text.** **`inkhaven language compose --kind`** generates **`names`**
  (phonotactic), **`prose`** (real grammatical sentences through the syntax
  engine), and **`poem`** (metered verse that scans). The themed kinds
  **`blessing`** / **`curse`** / **`incantation`** are AI-composed but
  *constrained to your existing lexicon* — the model arranges real words, never
  invents them — and print a native text with gloss and translation. Everything
  is printed, never written into your books.

## A guide that keeps up

*Developing a Constructed Language with Inkhaven*
([`Book/CONLANG_DEVELOPMENT/`](../../Book/CONLANG_DEVELOPMENT/)) gains coverage of
all of the above: new sections on sentences, negation, questions, relative
clauses, and coordination (Grammar), the gap finder (A healthy lexicon), and
interchange + creative text (Producing the books), with new term boxes, command
reference entries, and glossary terms.

## Design notes

- **Deterministic core, advisory AI.** The syntax engine, exporters, importers,

- **Backward compatible.** Every new construction is opt-in; existing paradigms,

# Inkhaven 1.3.2 — The Planning Board

_On top of 1.3.1 (Submission track).  1.3 fills the bookends of the writing
lifecycle; with pillar A done, 1.3.2 opens **pillar B** — the front, where
you work on **structure**.  It leads with **diagnosis, not card-shuffling**:
turning "something's wrong with my middle but I can't see it" into a
specific, objective finding.  Pure-Rust, no external apps, no new
dependencies.  Plan:
[PLANNING-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/PLANNING-1_PLAN.md); walkthrough:
[Tutorial 67](../Tutorials/67-planning-board.md)._

## Structure is the third axis

Inkhaven already had the **Timeline** (*when* things happen) and **Threads**
(*whether each arc pays off*). The Planning Board adds the orthogonal third:
**structure** — acts, beats, turning points, the shape of the rise and
fall. It references threads/timeline; it never re-implements them.

## Lay a framework, then diagnose

```sh
inkhaven plan init --framework save_the_cat
# three_act (default) | save_the_cat | story_circle | hero_journey | seven_point
```

Each beat is an HJSON paragraph in the new **Planning** system book (the
Threads pattern). Map one to a chapter by setting `mapped_chapter` (and the
`threads` it advances). Then:

```sh
inkhaven plan check        # deterministic — no AI; --json / --drift / --book-name
```

Three diagnoses, all objective:

- **Coverage** — which beats have a home, which are gaps.
- **Position drift** — a beat far from where the framework expects it ("your
  Midpoint lands at 64%, target 50%").
- **Pacing** — each act's *word share* vs. the framework's shape ("Act 1 is
  30% of your words — long"). The factual version of "the opening drags".

The act proportions resolve to the canonical shape (three-act → 25 / 50 /
25). Findings are prompts to think, not verdicts.

## See it, then ask the AI

**`Ctrl+V Shift+K`** opens the structure outline: every beat as a position
bar — `|` where the framework wants it, `●` where it lands — colour-coded
on-target / drift / gap, with act pacing and `↪N` thread chips.

**`inkhaven plan analyze`** (or `a` in the outline, which streams into the
AI pane) reads the structure qualitatively over the **1.3.1 book digest** —
mapping beats to chapters and naming the sag. Its prompt resolves through
the Prompts-book → `prompts.hjson` → built-in tiers.

## Threads do narrative work

A beat's `threads` connect structure to arcs: `plan check` surfaces them
(`↪`), flags a reference to a thread that doesn't exist, and — once you're
using thread-links — nudges about mapped beats that advance no tracked
thread.

# Inkhaven 1.3.20 — Complement clauses, and a deeper developer's guide

_A focused follow-on to 1.3.19's syntax engine: it adds the last classic syntax
construction, then substantially deepens the beginner's book about the whole
ConLang Suite. No new dependencies. Reference: [CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md)._

## Complement clauses — the syntax engine is complete

1.3.19 made a language *speak* (sentences, negation, questions, relative clauses,
coordination). 1.3.20 adds the one piece that was still missing:

- **Complement clauses.** **`inkhaven language complement`** builds a sentence
  whose object is a whole clause — "I know *that the bird sees the stone*". The
  matrix subject and verb (`--subject` / `--verb`) wrap an embedded clause
  (`--comp-subject` / `--comp-verb` / `--comp-object`) introduced by an optional
  complementizer (glossed `COMP`). Because the complement fills the matrix
  *object* slot, your word order positions it on its own — an SVO language prints
  it after the matrix verb (`mi tira ya kira nami patan`), a verb-final language
  before it (`mi ya kira patan nami tira`) — and the embedded clause still
  case-marks its own object.

That completes the syntax-depth set: **sentence → negation → questions → relative
clauses → coordination → complement clauses**, all driven by the same typology
answers and paradigms as a plain sentence.

The novice book ([`Book/CONLANG_DEVELOPMENT/`](../../Book/CONLANG_DEVELOPMENT/))

# Inkhaven 1.3.21 — Scripting the ConLang Suite from Bund

_RFC LANG-1 is complete (P1–P10). This release opens the whole ConLang Suite to
**Bund**, Inkhaven's scripting layer: a single script can now define, inspect,
generate, AI-author, and typeset an entire constructed language — fully
interchangeable with the JSON/CLI path. No new dependencies. Reference:
[CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md)._

## The `ink.lang.*` tree

The new `src/scripting/stdlib/lang.rs` exposes the engine as ~37 words. Every one
is also reachable as the shorter `lang.X` (the `ink.` prefix dropped).

- **Define a whole language from a script.** `lang.init`, `lang.add_word`, and
  `lang.define` (writes a phonology / grammar / morphology / typology / sample
  HJSON block under a chapter) build a language that is byte-for-byte identical to
  a hand-authored one — so you may use JSON/HJSON *or* Bund, freely mixed.

- **Inspect every layer** (`store_read`, allowed by default): `list`,
  `generate_word`, `syllabify`, `ipa`, `stress`, `tone`, `transliterate`,
  `gloss`, `paradigm`, `derive`, `agree`, `sentence`, `relative`, `complement`,
  `coordinate`, `stats`, `audit`, `query`, `gaps`, `sound_change`, `cognates`,
  `family_tree`, `names`, `prose`, `poem`. Structured results come back as native
  Bund dicts/lists (a sentence yields `{ surface, gloss, literal }`; `stats` the
  full profile).

- **Mutate** (`store_write`, default-denied): `remove_word`, `derive_add`,
  `grammar_set`, `idiom_add`, `metaphor_add`.

- **AI generation** (`ai_write`, default-denied, **advisory** — returns data,
  never auto-writes): `compose` (themed blessing / curse / incantation),
  `reconstruct` (a proto-form from cognates), `realism_check`, and
  `generate_lexicon` (forms from the deterministic generator, AI assigns meaning,
  the dedup gate runs — survivors returned for you to commit).

- **Produce files** (`fs_write`, default-denied): `dictionary`, `grammar_book`,
  and `font_build` (compiles UFO/TTF), plus `glyph_lint` (`fs_read`) and
  `glyph_draft` (AI-drafts a glyph SVG; needs both `fs_write` and `ai_write`).

## Building artefacts natively

Bund's `{ … }` is a lambda, not a dict, so `lang.dict` turns a flat
`[ key val key val … ]` list into a real dict. It is aliased to self-documenting
names — `word`, `rule`, `phoneme`, `block` — so a script reads like what it
builds (`[ "ipa" "k" "kind" "consonant" ] phoneme`). Hand a dict to `lang.define`
and it serialises to the same HJSON the book stores.

## Safety model

Each word is classified into the existing scripting policy categories:
read-only inspectors are `store_read` (allowed); book mutators are `store_write`;
the AI words are `ai_write`; the file producers are `fs_write` — all
default-denied, opted into per project via
`scripting: { enabled_categories: [ … ] }`. A word that needs two capabilities
(e.g. `glyph_draft` writes a file *and* calls the LLM) checks the second one at
run time. Paths are confined to the project root by the same sandbox as
`ink.fs.*`. The AI words stay **advisory** — they return data; a script commits
anything it keeps through the separately-gated `add_word`.

- The developer's guide *Developing a Constructed Language with Inkhaven* gains a

  boxes are recoloured pastel mint-green so they stand out from the cream callouts

- **Zero new dependencies.** The Bund layer reuses the existing `conlang::*`

- **Interchangeable.** A Bund-built language opens, inspects, and renders

# Inkhaven 1.3.22 — The ConLang Suite: Sociolinguistics & Contact

_A whole new pillar for the ConLang Suite (RFC LANG-2): a constructed language
stops being uniform and starts living among its speakers and its neighbours —
dialects and registers, borrowed words, linguistic areas, and the speech of the
particular people and places of your world. The key insight throughout: a
**dialect is a sound-change chain applied synchronically**, and a **loanword is a
phonotactic repair** — so the new features are mostly orchestration over the
LANG-1 engines. Deterministic core, advisory AI, no new dependencies. Reference:
[CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md)._

## Variation — dialects, registers, sociolects (P1)

A **variety** is a *delta* on the base language, declared in a `varieties` block
in the Grammar chapter: an `id`, a `kind` (`dialect` / `register` / `sociolect` /
`idiolect`), an `axis`, a `prestige`, an ordered list of `sound_changes` (SPE
notation — the same `AllophonyRule` engine as diachronics), and optional
suppletive `lexicon` overrides.

- **`language varieties <lang>`** lists each variety with its axis, prestige, and
  delta sizes.
- **`language lect <lang> <variety> --word | --text`** renders a form or a line
  *in* a variety (`kata` → `kada` under `t > d / V _ V`), and reports the
  base-to-variety difference.
- **`language dialects <lang> [--count N]`** prints the classic dialectology
  comparison table — each headword across the base and every variety (a trailing
  `*` marks a word override).

The headline realised: `conlang::variety::render_form` reuses
`diachronic::apply::derive_form` directly — a living variety is the historical
engine run *now* instead of across generations.

## Contact — borrowing (P2)

A loanword is a **phonotactic repair**. How a language nativises borrowings is
declared in a `loan_phonology` block in its Phonology chapter (`repair:
epenthesis | deletion`, an `epenthetic_vowel`, and `substitutions` for donor
sounds the recipient lacks).

- **`language borrow <recipient> --form W --from L [--gloss G] [--yes]`** adapts a
  donor word in two steps — **perceive** (apply substitutions, keep native
  sounds, map the rest to the nearest phoneme by sonority) and **repair**
  (consonant runs longer than the recipient's templates allow get the epenthetic
  vowel, or a consonant is deleted): `tras` → `tulasu`. With `--yes` and a
  `--gloss`, the adapted word joins the dictionary with the donor recorded in its
  etymology.

## Areal features — Sprachbund (P3)

Languages in contact converge on shared structures. A `contact` block in the
Grammar chapter declares membership in a linguistic area (`region`, `with`
neighbours, `areal_features`).

- **`language areal [lang]`** gives a per-language convergence overlay — each
  shared feature marked **converged** (`✓`), **shift** (`→`), or **adopt** (`+`)
  — or, with no language, the whole-region Sprachbund view. It is strictly
  advisory; it never rewrites the grammar.
- **`language family-tree`** now draws **horizontal contact edges**
  (`Eldar ⇄ Sindar`) alongside the vertical lines of descent.

## Speech communities & ecology (P4)

The worldbuilding-links sidecar now carries varieties: a Place speaks a particular
variety of its language (`link-place … --variety`), and a Character has a
**native variety** — the base of their idiolect (`link-character …
--native-variety`).

## Grammar-book output (P5)

When a language declares varieties or contact, its reference grammar
(`grammar-book`, both `md` and `typ`) grows two sections automatically: a

adaptation). The renderer stays engine-free; `cli::language::build_variation`

## Advisory AI (P6)

The AI proposes *choices*; the deterministic engine *applies and validates* them
— so forms stay legal and nothing is written without `--yes`. All key off the
project working language.

- **`language propose-dialect <lang> --describe "…" [--yes]`** — the model
  suggests a coherent set of sound changes + lexical swaps; each rule is validated
  against the inventory and previewed through the P1 engine; `--yes` writes the
  variety into the Grammar chapter.
- **`language propose-loans <recipient> --from <donor> --topic … --count N`** —
  proposes concepts a language would borrow in a domain, then the deterministic
  adapter nativises each (`stɔrm` → `sitarimi`).
- **`language areal-check <lang>`** — judges whether a declared Sprachbund is
  typologically plausible (the contact analogue of `realism-check`).

# Inkhaven 1.3.23 — Local Translation: the ConLang Suite learns to translate

_A constructed language can now be **translated** — English → conlang, conlang →
English, and conlang → conlang — fully offline, deterministically, and improving
as you correct it. This is the core of RFC LANG-3, re-architected (Amendment A1)
to be **Python-free, training-free, and zero new dependencies**: a conlang is a
closed, formally-described domain, so translation is mostly orchestration over the
LANG-1 engines plus retrieval over the binary's existing embedding + vector
stack. Reference: [CONLANG.md](../CONLANG.md)._

## Tier 1 — the rule-based translator (RBMT)

The deterministic spine, in `src/conlang/translate/`. Because a LANG-1 language
carries a complete formal description — phonemes, morphology, typology, and a
lexicon whose every headword has an English gloss — translation reuses the
machinery already built:

- **`language translate <lang> "<english>"`** maps each English word to a
  headword by its gloss and hands the clause to the LANG-1 **syntax engine**,
  which orders by `word_order`, case-marks by `alignment`, inflects via the
  morphology spec, and runs agreement. So a translation reorders and inflects for
  free: *the bird sees the stone* → `kira nami pata` (SVO) or `kira pata nami`
  (SOV) from the same lexicon. Parsing is **lexicon-aware** — the verb is found by
  meaning, an attributive adjective is recovered and agrees with its noun, and
  number flows through (*the birds see the stones* → `kirai nami patai`).
- **`language reverse <lang> "<surface>"`** goes back to English, un-inflecting
  each surface word against the lexicon's paradigm forms and re-agreeing English
  number and tense.
- **`language cross <from> <to> "<surface>"`** translates one conlang into another
  through an English pivot (exposed), so an SVO language's `kira nami pata`
  crosses into an SOV language as `turi moki vela`, reordered for free.

Every output carries a per-word **confidence and decision trace**; a word the
lexicon can't cover is marked `«word»` and listed.

## Tier 2 — retrieval (a translation memory), not a trained model

The original plan fine-tuned a neural model (and needed Python to train it).
**Amendment A1** replaces that with **retrieval**: for a closed conlang the corpus
*is* the knowledge, so it is looked up at translation time instead of baked into
weights — and the retrieval stack (`fastembed`, the HNSW vector store,
`tokenizers`, `ort`) already ships in the binary.

- **`language remember <lang> --english … --conlang …`** confirms a translation.
  It is reused **immediately, on the very next call** — no retraining, no
  threshold. An exact remembered pair becomes the primary (the rule-based reading
  is kept as an alternative); nothing is silently overridden.
- Near matches are **semantic**: each remembered source is embedded once (with the
  same model that powers manuscript search) and a translation matches by cosine —
  so *a soldier lifts his blade toward the sun* recalls a remembered *the warrior
  raises his sword to the sun* with no shared content words.
- **`language corpus <lang> [--yes]`** seeds the memory by translating a bundled
  English pool and keeping what the language fully covers; its acceptance rate and
  top-missing words read out lexicon maturity.
- **`language eval <lang>`** measures quality without a human reference:
  round-trip similarity (translate → reverse → compare) and coverage.
- **`language export-translation <lang>`** packages the whole system as a portable
  single-file **`.itm`** bundle (the memory + lexicon + manifest + README) to ship
  alongside a published work — browsable as a phrasebook, re-seedable into another
  project.

## Scripting

The full pipeline scripts from **Bund**: `lang.translate` (memory-aware),
`lang.reverse`, `lang.cross`, `lang.remember`, `lang.memory`, `lang.corpus`,
`lang.eval`, and `lang.export` — all aliased and policy-classified.

## Design notes

- **Python-free, training-free, zero new dependencies, no required downloads.**
  Every piece reuses what was already in the binary: the LANG-1 engines for the
  RBMT, `fastembed` + the vector store for semantic recall, `zip` + `chrono` for
  the export bundle.
- **Deterministic and advisory.** The rule-based core is pure; retrieval surfaces
  *alternatives* and only an author-confirmed exact match overrides — the author
  always sees and chooses.
- **Correction loop beats the original design.** A correction is an immediate
  datastore append, where the fine-tuned plan batched 100 corrections and a
  training run to do less.
- The neural-fluency tiers (a base NLLB via the in-tree `ort`, or candle LoRA) are
  now an **optional** later phase, taken up only if retrieval proves insufficient
  on real conlangs.

Also in this release: a small fix surfacing two previously-unread fields
(`Adaptation.ipa` in `borrow`, `Variety.note` in `varieties`) to clear dead-code
warnings.

to tell you about without expecting a reply: translation results, Bund script
output, and (in later cycles) lexicon proposals, variety renderings, and world
fact-checks. One message envelope, one channel, `Ctrl+B Tab` to reach it. Zero
new dependencies — it reuses the in-tree DuckDB, ratatui, Bund VM, and chord

# Inkhaven 1.3.25 — World Simulation

_Inkhaven gains an actual simulated world. A new **`inkhaven realworld`**
compiler turns a structured `world.hjson` into a coherent, physically-grounded
world — sky, terrain, climate, rivers, and settlements — materialized into a new
**World** system book, with a proposal queue that turns its cities into real
Place records you accept one by one. This is the first slice of RFC WORLD-4 (the
compiler half; the fact-checker follows). It also **completes RFC PANE-1**: the
Output pane gains its remaining actions and becomes the default launch view._

_Reference: [WORLD-4_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-4_PLAN.md) ·
[PANE-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/PANE-1_PLAN.md)_

> **Naming note.** The simulation RFC was authored as "WORLD-1", but WORLD-1/2/3
> are the shipped *consistency* pillar (facts / drift / world report, 1.3.8–1.3.11).
> The simulation track is **WORLD-4** — a different thing that *builds* a world
> rather than checking one.

## The world compiler — `inkhaven realworld`

Write a `world.hjson` at the project root (start one with `inkhaven realworld new
<name>`), then compile it. Five deterministic layers run in dependency order,
each a pure function of `(definition, seed)` — same inputs, same world, every
time:

1. **Astronomy** — closed-form planetary physics. Year length from Kepler's third
   law (in the planet's own days), with a flag when your declared calendar
   diverges from the computed year; daily insolation by latitude band; per-moon
   synodic periods and lunations; tidal forcing (a close light moon correctly
   out-tides a far heavy one); season markers anchored to your calendar.
2. **Geology** — seed → tectonic plates (Voronoi boundaries, classified
   convergent / divergent / transform from relative plate motion) → a procedural
   heightmap with mountain uplift along convergent belts → continents, sea
   coverage, mountain ranges, and mineral hints. Or **import a DEM**: point
   `geology.dem` at a heightmap PNG and the compiler uses your terrain instead.
3. **Climate** — a zonal model: global mean from the star's flux, the latitude
   profile from the astronomy insolation, elevation lapse from the heightmap;
   precipitation from the Hadley / Ferrel / Polar belts, modified by
   continentality and orographic rain shadows; Köppen-style biomes and the
   prevailing-wind bands.
4. **Hydrology** — the textbook D8 flow model: flow direction → rainfall-weighted
   accumulation → rivers with a Strahler-style order → lakes → watersheds →
   settlement priors (river mouths, confluences, fertile valleys).
5. **Demographics** — biome carrying-capacity sets the population; the hydrology
   priors become a Rank-Size settlement hierarchy of cities, towns, and villages,
   with plausible social role types.

Each layer **materializes** into the new **World** system book (10th, after
Artefacts) as structured paragraphs — `World / Astronomy`, `Geology`, `Climate`,
`Hydrology`, `Demographics` — and the heightmap is written as a grayscale PNG
asset. Re-compiling is idempotent (it updates in place, never duplicates), and
astronomy through hydrology are compiler-owned facts that re-assert each run.

```
inkhaven realworld new Velmaron
inkhaven realworld compile --layer astronomy
inkhaven realworld compile --layer geology --materialize
inkhaven realworld compile --layer climate --json
# … hydrology, demographics …
```

## The proposal queue — the author always wins

Demographics is the first layer that **proposes** rather than asserts. Its
settlements don't silently become Places; they enter a **proposal queue** with
deterministic, pronounceable names, and you decide:

```
inkhaven realworld propose                      # seed the queue from the world
inkhaven realworld proposals list               # review names + rationale
inkhaven realworld proposals accept <id>        # commit one as a Place
inkhaven realworld proposals reject <id>        # never re-proposed
inkhaven realworld proposals accept-all
inkhaven realworld places                       # the accepted Place ↔ World links
```

Accepting creates a prose Place under the **Places** book and records a **Place ↔
World cross-reference** (climate zone, biome, hydrology basis, coordinates) keyed
to it — the join the fact-checker will use. Re-running `propose` never
re-proposes a site you already accepted or rejected.

## In the editor — `Ctrl+B W`

`Ctrl+B W` opens the **World overview**: the definition, the compiled astronomy,
per-layer status, and whether it's materialized. It's an actionable hub:

- **`C`** compiles every layer, materializes them, and seeds the proposal queue.
- **`P`** opens the proposal queue — `↑↓` navigate, `Enter` accepts (commits the
  Place), `r` rejects.

So you can build and curate an entire world without leaving the editor.
*(Distraction-free / focus mode moved from `Ctrl+B W` to **`Ctrl+B Shift+W`** to
free the World prefix.)*

## PANE-1 completed — the Output pane comes of age

The Output pane (1.3.24) gains its remaining actions and is now the **default
right-side pane on a project's first launch** (returning to a project restores
whichever pane you left):

- **Per-kind `Enter`** — a `translation_result` inserts its target at the cursor,

- A bare Bund `print` / `println` is **mirrored into Output**, one message per

- New **`Ctrl+B D`** chord — a *deterministic* (rule-based) translation of the

# Inkhaven 1.3.26 — The World Fact-Checker

_The other half of the world simulation arrives. 1.3.25 gave Inkhaven a compiler
that builds a world; 1.3.26 gives it a **fact-checker** that reads your prose and
flags claims that don't fit the world you built — as you write. A messenger who
covers 600 km in three days, a blizzard in your tropical capital, a city ten
times bigger than the map can feed, three moons in a two-moon sky: the Output
pane tells you, quietly, while you keep typing. And a **magic ledger** lets you
declare the exceptions to physics your world allows, so the checker respects
them. This is RFC WORLD-4 Branch B (the fast track)._

_Reference: [WORLD-4_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-4_PLAN.md)_

## The magic ledger — declared exceptions to physics

Add a `magic:` block to `world.hjson`. Each rule names a `kind`, the check
categories it `covers`, and who/where it applies to:

```hjson
magic: {
    enabled: true
    rules: [
        {
            kind: "messenger_birds"
            covers: ["travel_time"]
            description: "Royal pelicans fly day and night with relays"
            applicable_to: { roles: ["royal_messenger"] }
        }
        {
            kind: "extended_lifespan"
            covers: ["character_age"]
            description: "Sun-priests live to 200"
            applies_to_role: "sun_priest"
            multiplier: 2.5
        }
    ]
}
```

The fact-checker consults the ledger **lazily** — only after it has a candidate
warning. If a rule covers that warning's category and applies, the warning is
suppressed with a note ("consistent with declared magic rule `messenger_birds`")
instead of nagging you forever. A one-time setup retires whole classes of false
positive. List the ledger with `inkhaven realworld magic`; it materializes into
`World / Magic Ledger`.

## The fact-checker — fast track

The checker reads prose for assertions about the world and verifies them. It's
deterministic and instant (no LLM), and it runs four categories today:

- **Travel time** — a sentence that states a distance *and* a duration implies a
  pace; implausible paces flag ("600 km in three days = 200 km/day, which far
  exceeds pre-industrial travel"). Pure prose — needs no world data.
- **Climate** — weather described at a known place that contradicts its climate
  zone (a blizzard at a tropical city).
- **Demographics** — a population stated for a place that diverges sharply from
  the modeled figure ("a city of two million" where the world supports ~40,000).
- **Astronomy** — a moon count that disagrees with the world's sky ("all three
  moons" when the world has two).

The climate and demographics checks resolve place names in your prose through a
**gazetteer** built from the Place ↔ World cross-references — the same links the
compiler records when you accept a city. So the loop closes: compile a world,
accept its cities, write about them, and the checker knows what they are.

### Real-time, as you write

When your project has a world, the fast track runs **automatically**: pause for a
few seconds on a paragraph and its findings appear in the **Output pane** (per
PANE-1) — no chord, no focus stolen, you keep writing. A re-check replaces the
paragraph's prior findings, so the pane always shows the current state and fixed
problems simply disappear.

Prefer to ask explicitly? **`Ctrl+B W` → `F`** fact-checks the open paragraph on
demand and flips you to Output. Headless? `inkhaven fact-check --text "…"` (or
`--paragraph <id>`) prints findings with severity icons. Findings carry a
severity — info (suppressed by magic), warning, contradiction.

## The editor hub — `Ctrl+B W`

The World overview gained two more actions, so it's a one-stop hub:

- **`C`** compile + materialize every layer + seed the proposal queue.
- **`P`** review and accept/reject the Place proposals.
- **`F`** fact-check the open paragraph.

## New dependencies

**None.** The magic ledger and the entire fast-track fact-checker reuse what's
already in tree (`regex`, the DuckDB stores, the PANE-1 Output pane). The world
compiler's `noise` + `delaunator` (1.3.25) are unchanged.

## Compatibility

Non-breaking and opt-in. The fact-checker only runs when a project has a
`world.hjson`; projects without one are completely unaffected and pay no cost.
The `magic:` block is optional. The Output, Places, and World books all work
exactly as before.

# Inkhaven 1.3.27 — The world, mapped (and a deeper checker)

_1.3.25 built a world; 1.3.26 read your prose against it. 1.3.27 **draws** the
world and makes the checker **deeper**. Your compiled world now renders to an
actual map (via [plakat](https://crates.io/crates/plakat)); the fact-checker
gains a slow LLM track, a cross-paragraph **coherence** pass, scope chords,
multilingual place-name matching, and graceful degradation when it isn't sure
what language you're writing in. The world definition grows real **geography /
hydrology / economy** blocks, and the repo ships a complete, ready-to-compile
**Earth**. This rounds out RFC WORLD-4 toward its P7 polish._

_Reference: [WORLD-4_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-4_PLAN.md) · Tutorials
[76 — Building a world](../Tutorials/76-building-a-world-realworld.md),
[77 — World maps and the fact-checker](../Tutorials/77-world-maps-and-fact-checking.md)_

## Maps — `inkhaven realworld map`

Your compiled world now renders to a map. Inkhaven emits a **MapSpec v2** from the
geology / climate / hydrology / demographics layers and hands it to the `plakat`
binary, which draws it — `plakat map --map-spec` loads our spec and skips its own
LLM entirely, so the cartography stays a pure function of your world and seed.

```
$ inkhaven realworld map
map · Aldoria (160×120 grid) · plakat 1.10.0
  features: assets/maps/world.features.png
  geojson:  assets/maps/world.geojson
  20 landmark(s) resolved, 20 Place coordinate(s) refined
```

Three artifacts land under `assets/maps/`: the **MapSpec** JSON, a rendered
**features PNG**, and a **GeoJSON** (coast, rivers, roads, landmarks). Mountain
ranges come from clustering the heightfield's high cells; rivers run their real
D8 watercourse (mouth from hydrology, source traced upstream); landmarks are your
largest settlements, coastal cities becoming ports. plakat's resolved landmark
positions are read back to **refine each accepted Place's coordinates**.

- **`--spec-only`** writes the MapSpec without invoking plakat.
- **`--no-ingest`** renders without touching Place coordinates.
- TUI: **`Ctrl+B W` → `M`**.
- plakat is **optional** — a missing binary degrades to a notice, never a
  failure. Install with `cargo install plakat`.

## A deeper fact-checker

### The slow track — `fact-check --slow`

Where the fast track is deterministic patterns, the **slow track** asks the
configured LLM for the subtle contradictions patterns miss. It's opt-in and
cost-controlled: a **cost preflight** prints the estimated tokens and the day's
tally before each call, a per-call **soft cap** (`--max-cost`, default 6000;
`--force` overrides) refuses an oversized call, a daily ceiling holds, and
transient errors (rate limits, timeouts, 5xx) **retry with backoff**. A missing
provider or a reached cap degrades to a notice.

### Coherence — `realworld coherence <node>`

A new pass checks a *run* of paragraphs **against each other** — a character in
two places without the travel between, a fact asserted then reversed, a timeline
that doesn't add up. Give it a book or chapter node id; it gathers the paragraphs
in document order and runs one cost-capped call, citing the `¶` numbers involved.

### Scope chords — `Ctrl+B W` → `F` → `P` / `B` / `R`

`F` now arms a scope picker: check the open **p**aragraph, the whole enclosing
**b**ook, or the 12 most **r**ecently edited paragraphs. Each pass replaces those
paragraphs' prior Output findings and flips you there with a summary.

### Idle auto slow-check — `Ctrl+B W` → `S`

An opt-in toggle (off by default — it spends tokens). With it on, ~45 s of quiet
on a changed paragraph runs the slow track **in the background**; the editor stays
responsive and findings land in Output when ready.

### An economy category

The fast track gains a fifth category — a metal mined or worked in the prose that
the world's geology doesn't yield, scoped to a clear extraction context so a
silver ring doesn't imply local silver.

## Multilingual matching & graceful degradation

- **Grammatical variants** — place names now resolve in their inflected forms.
  The win is Russian declension (`в Москве` / `к северу от Москвы` both match
  `Москва`); German adds its genitive `-s`.
- **Never-fail detection** — language detection reports a **confidence**; when it
  isn't sure, the checker renders the warning in English rather than asserting a
  guessed language. It never panics on any input.
- **Honest backend** — the optional enhanced parser (a UD model) is *never
  required*; an absent or unreadable asset silently degrades to the built-in
  heuristic, and the fact-check footer names the active backend (`INKHAVEN_LANG_MODEL`
  points at an enhanced one).

## Author-declared setting blocks

The world definition gains three optional blocks — and expanded geology — that
let you name your world's real features. They materialize into a **Setting**
chapter of the World book, and two of them feed the checker directly:

```hjson
geography: { landmarks: [ { name: "Cairo", kind: "city", climate_zone: "hot_desert", population: 9500000 } ] }
economy:   { tech_level: "industrial", resources: [ "iron", "copper", "petroleum" ] }
hydrology: { rainfall: "temperate", rivers: [ { name: "Nile" } ] }
geology:   { generated: { volcanism: "moderate", mineral_richness: "rich", notable_minerals: [ "iron", "gold" ] } }
```

- A **landmark** with a `climate_zone` becomes a gazetteer entry the checker
  resolves by name — *before* you compile and accept procedural Places. "Snow
  fell on Cairo" flags against its declared `hot_desert` zone.
- `economy.resources` + `geology.notable_minerals` join the checker's known
  goods, so trading your world's ores isn't flagged.

The repo ships [`examples/realworld/Earth.hjson`](../../examples/realworld/Earth.hjson)
— a complete, heavily-commented real Sun/Earth/Moon definition: exact astronomy,

The `Ctrl+B W` panel no longer claims the geology / climate / hydrology /

# Inkhaven 1.3.28 — Inner Socrates

_Inkhaven gains a third examined-authorship pillar. The ConLang Suite examines your
languages; the world simulator examines your world; **Inner Socrates examines your
prose** — reading alongside you and surfacing **questions** about the assumptions it
treats as given, the framings it presupposes, the tensions inside it, what each scene
does for the work. It is non-prescriptive by structural commitment: every finding is
a question, never a correction. You examine your prose; Inner Socrates never edits it.
This is RFC INNER_SOCRATES-1, built end to end in this release._

_Reference: [INNER_SOCRATES.md](../INNER_SOCRATES.md) · Plan:
[INNER_SOCRATES-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/INNER_SOCRATES-1_PLAN.md) · Tutorial:
[78 — Examined authorship with Inner Socrates](../Tutorials/78-inner-socrates.md)_

## Two tracks, fifteen questions

Like the world fact-checker, Inner Socrates runs a **Fast track** (deterministic,
instant, no LLM) and a **Slow track** (the configured LLM, cost-capped). Both
consult the active Reader Persona and the intent ledger, and both surface to the
**Output pane**.

- **Fast track (7 categories)** — asserted necessity, hedging, structural patterns,
  unattributed dialogue, sentence length, tense shifts, pronoun ambiguity. Runs on
  a writing pause (opt-in) or `Ctrl+B J → F`, in five languages.
- **Slow track — prose (5)** — hidden assumptions, internal tensions, framings,
  significance, structural echoes.
- **Slow track — timeline (3)** — dramatization gaps (events the timeline names but
  no paragraph depicts), implications left untraced, temporal density. `inner-socrates
  timeline` reads the prose against the project's events.

Three severities — **Notice** (hidden by default), **Inquiry** (the visible bulk),
**Probe** (structural, always visible) — mapped onto the Output pane.

## Reader Personas

Five bundled perspectives, each calibrated to read differently: **Inner Socrates**
(the default), **The Careful Editor**, **The Skeptical Reader**, **The First-Time
Reader**, **The Slow Reader**. Author your own as an HJSON file (`persona new`, or
`Ctrl+B J → N` for an AI-guided wizard); they live in `~/.config/inkhaven/personas/`
(cross-project) or the Intent book (project). `Ctrl+B J → S` cycles the active one.

## The intent ledger

The prose counterpart of the world simulator's **magic ledger** — same vocabulary
(Entry, Kind, Coverage, Scope, lazy Consultation, Suppression, Promotion). A
declared deliberate choice (a deliberate ambiguity, a framing, a structural echo, a
temporal gap) **suppresses** a would-be finding. Entries accumulate two ways: you
declare them, or the **promotion mechanism** suggests one after you dismiss the same
kind of finding five times. Carry series-level intentions to the next book with the
**`.isl` bundle** (`bundle export` / `import`).

## Surfaces

- **`Ctrl+B J`** — the Inner Socrates hub: `F` fast-check · `C` converse with the
  persona · `N` new-persona wizard · `S` cycle persona · `L` ledger · `A` toggle the
  ambient auto-check. (`Ctrl+B I` stays book-info.)
- **CLI** — `inkhaven inner-socrates check [--slow] · timeline · ledger · persona
  … · suggestions … · bundle … · findings …`.
- **Bund** — read-only `ink.inner_socrates.*` words (`check.fast`, `findings.list`,
  `personas.list`, `persona.active`, `ledger.list`, `usage.today`).
- A new **Intent system book** (the 13th) seeds on project init.

## Multilingual & cost

Five languages (EN/RU/ES/FR/DE) inherited from the world simulator: the Fast track
detects the paragraph's language, runs its marker table, and renders the question in
it — degrading to English when unsure. The Slow track reuses the cost preflight,
soft/daily caps, and retry-with-backoff, under a separate `inner_socrates_llm_usage`
sub-budget. The Fast track needs no provider; a missing one degrades to a notice.

## Also in this release

The **WORLDBUILDING.md** reference guide for the world simulator (RFC WORLD-4) — the
field-by-field companion to tutorials 76/77, completing WORLD-4's documentation.

## Dependencies & compatibility

**Zero new dependencies** — everything is inherited from the Output pane and the
world simulator (the language detector, the cost/retry helpers, the ledger pattern,
the background-job harness). Non-breaking and opt-in: nothing runs unless you invoke
it (or enable the ambient check). Every finding is a question, never a correction.

# Inkhaven 1.3.29 — Inner Socrates, in conversation

_A focused follow-on to 1.3.28's Inner Socrates: the Socratic interrogator becomes
**interactive**. The conversation gains a proper F9 scope, and every finding in the
Output pane gains the outcomes a careful reader's note deserves — declare it
deliberate, write it down, or mark it handled. This completes RFC INNER_SOCRATES-1's
interactive layer._

_Reference: [INNER_SOCRATES.md](../INNER_SOCRATES.md) · Plan:
[INNER_SOCRATES-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/INNER_SOCRATES-1_PLAN.md)_

## The Socrates F9 scope

The AI pane's **F9** scope cycle now includes **Socrates**, after Facts:

```
None → Selection → Paragraph → Subchapter → Chapter → Book → Facts → Socrates → None
```

Cycling into Socrates is a sticky **conversation** scope: it seeds the chat with the
active Reader Persona's voice and the open paragraph's questions, then hands you the
prompt. The persona discusses the work *with* you — it never drafts your prose. The
scope label shows in the AI-pane header; re-cycling refreshes the seed. It's the same
conversation `Ctrl+B J → C` opens, now reachable through the standard scope cycle.

## Per-finding outcomes

A Socratic question in the **Output pane** is no longer just something to read and
dismiss. With one selected:

- **`i`** — *record as intent*: declare the finding's category a deliberate choice
  (scoped to its chapter). Inkhaven writes an intent-ledger entry and stops asking
  that question here.
- **`m`** — *make note*: turn the question into a Notes entry, under a new
  **Socratic Notes** chapter, quoting the question and the passage with room for your
  response — the thinking captured where you'll find it again.
- **`x`** — *mark addressed*.
- **`d`** — *dismiss* (still feeds the promotion mechanism — five dismissals of the
  same kind, and Inkhaven offers to declare it for you).

Each outcome dismisses the message once it's handled, and the Output footer
advertises them for Socratic findings.

## Dependencies & compatibility

**Zero new dependencies.** Non-breaking and opt-in. Every finding remains a question,
never a correction. Tests 1713 (stable; one cycle-order test updated for the new
scope).

# Inkhaven 1.3.30 — The fact-checker learns *when*

_The world fact-checker knew what your world looks like — its geography, climate,
demographics, economy. It didn't know **when** each scene happens. 1.3.30 connects
it to your **timeline**: now a paragraph linked to an event (or near one in
world-time) is checked against ground truth, not prose inference. The messenger who
outran the calendar, the snow in a summer-dated scene, the character in two cities
at once — the checker catches them. This is RFC WORLD-5, built end to end, purely
additive to WORLD-4._

_Reference: [WORLDBUILDING.md](../WORLDBUILDING.md) §Timeline-aware checking · Plan:
[WORLD-5_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-5_PLAN.md) · Tutorial:
[80 — Timeline-aware fact-checking](../Tutorials/80-timeline-aware-fact-checking.md)_

## What the timeline adds

When your project has a [timeline](../Tutorials/31-story-timeline.md), the existing
fast checker gains four kinds of question — all running automatically (`Ctrl+B W →
F` or the ambient check), in five languages, and respecting the **magic ledger**
exactly like the world checks:

- **Calendar-grounded season** — weather contradicting the timeline-dated season
  is now a **contradiction** (snow in a paragraph the timeline places in summer),
  not a guess.
- **Event-derived travel time** — a prose "three days" that contradicts the gap
  between the traveller's events (say 35 days) is flagged. *The flagship example.*
- **`date_coherence`** (new category) — a seasonal date-hint in the prose (a
  *midsummer feast*, a *harvest*, a solstice) contradicting the dated season.
- **`co_location`** (new category) — a character whose events place them in two
  *different* places at overlapping times. Check the whole timeline at once with
  `inkhaven realworld co-location`.

Timeline-derived findings carry a **📅** marker in the Output pane so you can tell
the timeline was consulted. A `weather_control` or `teleportation` magic rule
covering the category suppresses the finding with a note, just like every other
check.

## Surfaces

- **TUI** — runs automatically into the Output pane with the existing fact-check
  chords; no new chords.
- **CLI** — `fact-check` gains `--timeline-aware auto|on|off` (default `auto` —
  on when the project has a timeline) and `--timeline-only`; plus `inkhaven
  realworld co-location`.
- **Bund** — five read-only `ink.world.fact_check.timeline.*` words (`events_near`,
  `events_for_character`, `events_for_place`, `season_for`, `effective_date`).

The legacy timeline AI critique (1.2.6+) still runs unchanged; during this interim
the two may overlap — lean on the fact-checker and don't invoke the legacy critique

# Inkhaven 1.3.32 — Project doctor

_1.3.x has been a feature explosion — the ConLang Suite, WORLD-4/5, INNER_SOCRATES-1,
TIMELINE-2-INTEGRATION. 1.3.32 opens the road to **1.4.0**, a consolidation &
hardening milestone, and it opens with the stability bookend: a data-integrity
safety net and the test/bench spine every release after it will lean on. The
`inkhaven doctor` scanner learns **referential integrity**, and the codebase gains
a property-based test harness over its panic-prone parsers._

_Plan: [DOCTOR_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/DOCTOR_PLAN.md) · Roadmap:
[ROADMAP-1.4.0.md](../PROPOSALS/ROADMAP-1.4.0.md) · Maintenance:
[MAINTENANCE.md](../MAINTENANCE.md)_

## Doctor learns referential integrity

`inkhaven doctor --scan` already caught disk-side trouble (zero-byte files, orphan
rows, bdslib drift, corrupt sidecars). None of its checks looked at the **dangling
UUIDs inside the hierarchy** — the references that rot from deletes, partial
restores, and hand-edits. Five new classes close that gap, all running on the
already-loaded node tree (no extra I/O):

- **`broken-parent-ref`** *(Critical)* — a node whose `parent_id` points at a UUID
  that doesn't exist. The node is detached — unreachable from the tree, invisible in
  the TUI. Real structural corruption.
- **`dangling-paragraph-link`** *(Warning)* — a `linked_paragraphs` entry whose
  target paragraph was deleted.
- **`dangling-event-ref`** *(Warning)* — a timeline event referencing a
  character/place node that no longer exists.
- **`sibling-slug-collision`** *(Warning)* — two children of the same parent sharing
  a slug, so their on-disk paths collide (one overwrites the other on save /
  assemble).
- **`duplicate-system-book`** *(Warning)* — more than one Book carrying the same
  `system_tag`, which makes system-book lookups ambiguous.

They run in the default `doctor --scan` (and gate CI: exit code 2 on any
≥ Warning), are addressable individually with `--class <name>`, and appear in
`--json` output. Detection-only this release — the safe autofixes (pruning dangling
refs) are a planned follow-up.

## A property-test spine

The road to 1.4.0 needs a stability backbone, so 1.3.32 stands one up:

- **`proptest`** (a pure-Rust dev-dependency) for property-based testing.
- **Perf budgets as ordinary tests** — an in-process timing assertion that runs in
  the normal `cargo test` gate (the right tool for catching a regression, vs.
  criterion for manual profiling). First budget: the referential scans over a
  1,000-node project complete well under half a second, guarding against an
  accidental O(n²).
- **A parser property sweep** codifying *never-panic* guarantees on the three
  panic-prone parsers — the calendar (`parse` / `format` / round-trip across every
  preset and precision), HJSON config loading (arbitrary input *and* brace/quote
  soup — a panic there would crash the editor at open), and language detection
  (arbitrary unicode, empty / emoji / 100k-char inputs).

## Dependencies & compatibility

**No external application or binary dependencies.** One pure-Rust dev-crate
(`proptest`), test-only — never linked into the shipped binary. No change to the
data model, the CLI surface, or any existing scan class. Tests 1725 → 1771.
