# Inkhaven 1.3.33 — Command palette + a filterable Output pane

_Two quality-of-life features on the road to 1.4.0, both about finding things fast.
The **command palette** gives you one chord to fuzzy-find and run any of Inkhaven's
many commands without remembering its keystroke. The **Output pane** — which now
collects findings from five-plus subsystems on one surface — gains **filtering** so
a busy pane narrows to what you care about. Both are pure additions over existing
infrastructure; zero new external dependencies._

_Plans:
[PALETTE_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/PALETTE_PLAN.md) ·
[OUTPUT_FILTER_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/OUTPUT_FILTER_PLAN.md) · Roadmap:
[ROADMAP-1.4.0.md](../PROPOSALS/ROADMAP-1.4.0.md)_

## The command palette

`Ctrl+B`'s chord tree has grown large. The command palette is the fast way through
it: **`Ctrl+V Space`** opens a fuzzy finder over **every** command — type to filter
by name, chord, or description; `↑↓` to select; `Enter` runs it; `Esc` closes.

- It's a projection of the live keybinding registry, so it always reflects your
  actual bindings (including HJSON / `ink.key.*` overrides) and **self-lists** —
  the palette command appears in the palette.
- Bound to **`Ctrl+V Space`** (a two-key chord with no `Ctrl+Shift+<letter>`
  terminal ambiguity — `Ctrl+P` is the editor paste, untouched).
- Discoverable: it's listed in the **Quick reference** (`Ctrl+B H`), which also
  gains a `?` shortcut to open it from the Tree pane.

## A filterable Output pane

The Output pane gathers structured findings from the world fact-checker, Inner
Socrates, the timeline critique, translation, the lexicon, Bund, and more. When it
gets busy, three filter dimensions narrow it — the title shows `shown/total · <filter>`,
and the filter **persists across restarts** (in `.session.json`):

- **`f`** — cycle by **source**: fact-check / socrates / timeline-critique / world /
  translation / lexicon / variety / ai / bund / other. (A source classifier maps
  every message kind to one clean group — there was never a single provenance field
  to filter on.)
- **`S`** — cycle by **minimum severity** (Info / Warning / Contradiction); also
  hides transient progress ticks.
- **`t`** — **this paragraph only**: just the messages tied to the open paragraph.
- **`c`** — clear all filters.

The pane and its key handler share one filtered view, so selection and per-message
actions always match what's on screen. Release notes also document the Output pane's
existing keys for the first time (KEYBINDING §4.1).

## Surfaces & docs

- **TUI** — `Ctrl+V Space` palette; `f` / `S` / `t` / `c` in the Output pane; `?`
  opens the Quick reference from the Tree pane.
- **Docs** — `KEYBINDING.md` gains the palette rows + a new §4.1 Output pane
  section; the in-app Quick reference lists both.
- **Diagnostics** — an opt-in `INKHAVEN_KEYLOG=1` key tracer (logs each key's
  `code/modifiers/kind` to `.inkhaven.log`) for debugging terminal-specific chord
  reporting.

## Dependencies & compatibility

**No external application or binary dependencies; no new runtime crates.** Both
features are read-side views over existing infrastructure — the keybinding registry
and the Output message store are unchanged. Legacy `.session.json` files (without
the filter key) load cleanly with filtering off. Tests 1771 → 1795.

# Inkhaven 1.3.34 — The review pass, and where the money goes

_Two road-to-1.4.0 consolidation features. **`inkhaven check`** is the unified review
pass: one gesture runs every fast checker over a scope and lights up the manuscript
with where attention is needed. The **AI cost dashboard** is one place to see today's
LLM spend — now tracking **every** inference, not just the capped slow tracks — and
it follows the house rule that cost control should **inform, not gate**. Both are
pure additions over existing infrastructure; zero new dependencies._

_Plans: [CHECK_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/CHECK_PLAN.md) ·
[COST_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/COST_PLAN.md) · Roadmap:
[ROADMAP-1.4.0.md](../PROPOSALS/ROADMAP-1.4.0.md)_

## The unified review pass

Each checker used to be its own command. **`Ctrl+B Shift+C`** (or `inkhaven check`)
now runs them all at once:

- the **world fact-checker** + **Inner Socrates** over the open paragraph,
- the **timeline critique** over the project,

all into the **Output pane** — where the 1.3.33 filtering (`f`/`S`/`t`) slices the
combined findings — with a `fact N · socrates N · timeline N` summary. Instant and
LLM-free.

And the manuscript shows you **where** to look: each tree node carries a
**report-card badge** (`⊗`/`⚠`/`●` + count) for the open findings under it,
aggregated up from the source paragraphs and colored by the worst severity. The
count drops as you dismiss findings.

CLI: `inkhaven check [--paragraph … | --book-name …] [--no-fact | --no-socrates |
--no-timeline]` prints the same findings grouped + a per-checker summary.

## The AI cost dashboard

**`Ctrl+B $`** (or `inkhaven cost`) opens one view of today's LLM usage:

- **Daily budgets** (the cost-capped slow tracks) with a usage bar.
- **Other AI calls today**, by category — chat, grammar, explain, critique,
  continuation, translation, and the rest. Every inference is now recorded at the
  one chokepoint it flows through, so this is the *whole* picture, not just the
  capped tracks.
- Today's total.

The counts are **per calendar day (UTC)** and reset at 00:00 UTC. The dashboard is
extensible: any future analytical thread that records a slow pass under its own
sub-budget appears automatically.

### Cost control informs; it does not gate

Following Inkhaven's design principle — a permissive individual tool, restricting
only for security — **the daily caps no longer block.** Past a daily budget the
slow tracks **warn and continue**; the author decides. The dashboard says so
plainly: *"Budgets are informative, not limits."*

## Surfaces & docs

- **TUI** — `Ctrl+B Shift+C` review pass; `Ctrl+B $` cost dashboard; tree badges;
  both self-list in the command palette + quick reference.
- **CLI** — `inkhaven check`, `inkhaven cost`.
- **Docs** — KEYBINDING §1.1 gains an "Any pane" table (the review pass + the cost
  dashboard); KEYBINDING §4.1 (the Output pane) was added in 1.3.33.

## Dependencies & compatibility

**No external application or binary dependencies; no new runtime crates.** Both
features are read-side views/orchestration over existing checkers and stores. The
one behavioural change is making the previously-blocking daily slow-track cap a
warning. Tests 1795 → 1804.

# Inkhaven 1.3.35 — Keeping count

_Writing goals were always **~90% built** — the streak engine, per-book pacing,
daily targets, status-ladder, active-time, and the `Ctrl+V g` progress modal all
shipped long ago. This release finishes the job: it **surfaces** goals in the
terminal, **extends** the streak to a lifetime record, and makes goals **editable
in-app** without leaving the keyboard — each a pure addition over existing
infrastructure, zero new dependencies._

_Plan: [GOALS_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/GOALS_PLAN.md) · Roadmap:
[ROADMAP-1.4.0.md](../PROPOSALS/ROADMAP-1.4.0.md)_

## `inkhaven goals` — the terminal surface

Every other analytic — `cost`, `check`, `stats`, `concordance` — had a terminal
counterpart; the writing-progress view did not. **`inkhaven goals`** prints the
same picture the `Ctrl+V g` modal shows, reusing the *exact* `build_snapshot`
engine (no goal logic duplicated):

- project + per-book word totals,
- today vs `goals.daily_words` with a usage bar,
- current streak (with grace) **and lifetime best**,
- per-book required pace + days-to-deadline,
- this week's status-ladder promotions,
- active time today / week, and a 30-day sparkline.

Read-only; it records nothing and changes no config — handy for scripts, cron
digests, or a glance without opening the TUI.

## The streak you keep — lifetime best + milestones

The streak figure only ever knew the trailing run, and the heatmap's "longest" was
**window-bound** — it forgot. Now the snapshot computes a true **all-time best**
over the project's full writing history (same grace rule), shown as `· best Nd` in
both `inkhaven goals` and the progress modal whenever it beats the current run.

And crossings are worth marking: a new Bund hook **`hook.on_streak_milestone
( milestone_days -- )`** fires the first time the current streak crosses **7 / 30 /
100 / 365** days upward (the highest newly reached). Reopening a project already
past a milestone doesn't re-fire. In keeping with the house rule, it's an
**informative celebration — never blocking**. Documented in the Bund tutorial + the
cheat sheet.

## Editing goals in-app — and writing them back safely

Setting a goal used to mean hand-editing `inkhaven.hjson`. Now press **`e`** inside
the `Ctrl+V g` progress modal to open the **goals editor**: adjust
`goals.daily_words`, `active_minutes_daily`, and `streak_grace_per_week` inline
(`↑↓` field · digits · `Enter` save · `Esc` cancel). The change applies to the live
config immediately — no restart.

The write is the careful part. `Config::save` would full-rewrite the file and
**drop every comment** — unacceptable for a hand-tuned config. Instead the commit
routes through Inkhaven's existing **comment-preserving surgical-splice** pipeline:

- a **versioned backup** of the pre-patch file lands in `.config-backups/` first,
- only the **changed** keys are spliced (present) or appended (absent),
- the file is written **atomically** (`.tmp` + rename).

Every comment, every unrelated stanza, every unknown field survives byte-for-byte.
This is the **permissive principle** in practice: a writer's own config is never
clobbered, and there is always a backup.

## Housekeeping

Two never-used symbols (`ai::usage::uninstall`, `store::SYSTEM_TAG_INTENT`) were
removed to clear the build warnings. Clean build.

## Surfaces & docs

- **TUI** — `Ctrl+V g` now shows lifetime best; press `e` for the goals editor.
- **CLI** — `inkhaven goals`.
- **Hook** — `hook.on_streak_milestone`.
- **Docs** — KEYBINDING (the `Ctrl+V g` row + `e` editor), quick reference, Bund
  tutorial + cheat sheet.

## Dependencies & compatibility

**No external application or binary dependencies; no new runtime crates.** All three
increments are additions over the existing progress engine and the config-TUI's
splice pipeline. No on-disk shape moved; the new `goals.*` keys are the same ones
the config already understood. Tests 1804 → 1813.

# Inkhaven 1.3.36 — Every snapshot, and a lock on the door

_The snapshot **browser** finally lets you look across your whole project's history, not
just the open paragraph's. Alongside it, the first slice of the road-to-1.4.0
**hardening sweep**: never-panic fuzz coverage for the parsers that read untrusted
files, and an advisory **project lock** that guards the store against two sessions at
once — informing, never blocking. Plus two fixes to the 1.3.35 goals editor. All pure
additions over existing infrastructure; the lock reuses a dependency already present._

_Plan: [SNAPSHOT_HARDENING_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/SNAPSHOT_HARDENING_PLAN.md) · Roadmap:
[ROADMAP-1.4.0.md](../PROPOSALS/ROADMAP-1.4.0.md)_

## The project-wide snapshot browser

`F6` has always shown the open paragraph's snapshots. **`Ctrl+F6`** now opens a
**project-wide browser** — every snapshot across *all* paragraphs, newest first, one
row each (timestamp · words · paragraph · annotation):

- `↑↓` moves; the list scrolls with a cursor-following window.
- `/` filters by **paragraph title or annotation** (case-insensitive; Enter/Esc leaves
  the filter, a second Esc closes).
- `V` diffs the selection against its paragraph's **current** text — the same
  side-by-side diff modal `F6` uses, returning to the browser on Esc.
- `Enter` opens that paragraph and drops you into its `F6` picker, where load / restore /
  pin live.

Built on the existing snapshot engine: a new `Store::list_all_snapshots()` (the
per-paragraph query minus its parent filter) feeding the proven `compute_line_diff` +
diff modal. Available from any pane; self-lists in the command palette.

## Hardening — parser fuzzing

The importers that read **untrusted external files** now carry never-panic property
tests, in the same style as the existing calendar/config sweeps:

- **Scrivener RTF** (`rtf_to_typst` + the plain-text fallback) — arbitrary bytes and an
  RTF control-word/brace/prose token-salad.
- **Typst syntax check** (`check`) — arbitrary Unicode source and a markup-delimiter
  salad, exercising the byte-offset → line/col mapping over multibyte input.
- **Scrivener `.scrivx` binder XML** (`parse_scrivx`) — arbitrary bytes and an XML
  tag/attribute salad with unbalanced and mis-nested tags through `quick_xml`.

Seven new proptests, ~256 cases each. They surfaced **no panics** — so the parsers were
already robust; this locks that in against regressions.

## Hardening — the advisory project lock

Two `inkhaven` sessions open on the same project both write `metadata.db` and
`.session.json`; interleaved writes can corrupt the store. A new lock guards against
that **without ever hard-blocking** — true to Inkhaven's permissive principle, it
*informs* and the author decides:

- An **OS advisory lock** (`flock` / `LockFileEx`) on `<project>/.inkhaven.lock`. The
  kernel releases it on exit, crash, or `kill -9`, so there is **no stale-lock cleanup**
  to get wrong — a dead session never locks anyone out.
- On launch, if another live session holds it, you get a clear warning naming the other
  process and an **"Open anyway? [y/N]"** prompt. Decline leaves the existing session
  untouched; accept proceeds. A filesystem without advisory locks, or any lockfile
  error, simply proceeds — infrastructure never blocks you.

CLI subcommands stay unlocked: they're short-lived and intentional.

## Goals-editor fixes (from 1.3.35)

- **Backspace now deletes** in the goals editor. Some terminals report the Backspace key
  as a control char rather than `KeyCode::Backspace`; the editor now accepts all the
  encodings (and `Delete`).
- A `0` ("disabled") field seeds as **empty** (still rendered as `0`), so you type the
  new target cleanly instead of deleting a stuck `0` first.
- The `Ctrl+B Shift+G` heatmap now opens the goals editor on **`e`** too — the natural
  place to want to adjust a target.

## Dependencies & compatibility

**No external application or binary dependencies; no new runtime crates** — the lock
reuses `fs2`, already in the tree. No on-disk shape moved; `.inkhaven.lock` is a new,
self-managing dotfile. The fuzz tests are dev-only. Tests 1813 → 1825.

# Inkhaven 1.3.4 — The Planning Board: the shape of the rise and fall

_On top of 1.3.3. 1.3.2 diagnosed where each beat **lands**; 1.3.3 made
mapping **fluent**. 1.3.4 adds the two things the Board still couldn't
see — **intensity** (a tension curve) and **scene-level** craft (scene
cards) — plus the deferred outline interactions. Full plan:
[PLANNING-3_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/PLANNING-3_PLAN.md)._

## Headline

- **Tension curve** — every beat now carries an *expected* intensity (the
  framework's authored dramatic shape) measured against an *actual*
  intensity derived from the manuscript, so a sagging middle is an
  objective finding ("Midpoint: tension 33% where the framework wants
  65%"), not a vibe. Deterministic — no render-time AI.
- **Scene cards** — a finer grain than beats: each scene's
  goal → conflict → disaster, with a deterministic weak-scene check (a
  scene that states a goal but never turns).
- **Interactive outline, finished** — the deferred `t` (thread-link) and
  `Enter` (jump-to-chapter) keys, plus `v` for the scene board.

## The tension curve

Beat **placement** (drift, pacing) was 1.3.2's story; **intensity** is
1.3.4's. A midpoint can land at exactly 50% and still be flat.

- **Expected** is authored canon, like `target_position`: every beat of all
  five frameworks gets an `expected_tension` — calm open, peak in the back
  half, the canonical rise and fall.
- **Actual** is *open narrative-obligation density* — the count of debts in
  the air at each point, derived deterministically from data you already
  keep: the **tension ledger** (`inkhaven tension scan`'s introduced /
  resolved tags) and your open **Threads** (weighted by each arc's
  tension). A question raised but unpaid keeps the line high.

Where expected is high but actual is low, the beat is flagged **flat**.
`inkhaven plan check` prints a **TENSION** section (and `--json` carries the
curve); the **`Ctrl+V Shift+K`** outline draws expected + actual as
block-ramp sparklines (`▁`..`█`) aligned under the position bars, so a
beat's `●` sits over its actual-tension cell. With no scan and no linked
threads you still get the expected shape, with a hint.

## Scene cards

Beats are chapter-scale; scene cards work one level down — each scene's
**goal → conflict → disaster** (Swain). The deterministic check is the
**turn**: a scene that states a goal but has no disaster doesn't turn.

- `inkhaven plan scene add <title> --chapter <slug> [--goal … --conflict …
  --disaster …]`, `plan scene list` (grouped by chapter with G/C/D marks +
  weak flags), `plan scene set`, `plan scene remove`. Cards live under a
  **Scenes** chapter of the Planning book.
- Folded into `plan check` (a SCENES section + the no-turn findings) and
  surfaced in the outline: press **`v`** for the scene board.
- `plan analyze` reads the cards too — it names the scenes that don't turn
  and suggests the missing turn.

## Interactive outline, finished

The `Ctrl+V Shift+K` outline gains the deferred 1.3.3 interactions:

- **`t`** — link threads to the selected beat (Space toggles each).
- **`Enter`** — open the beat's mapped chapter in the editor.
- **`v`** — flip to the scene board.

joining `m` (map), `s` (status), and `a` (analyze) from 1.3.3.

## Under the hood

- Zero new dependencies — the curve is pure arithmetic over the existing
  ledger / threads / chapter positions; scene cards reuse the HJSON-
  paragraph write-back.
- New pure, unit-tested helpers: `planning::tension_curve`,
  `intensity_sparkline`, `analyze_scenes`, `tension::obligation_spans`.
- Tests 1307 → 1316. One tutorial refreshed (67).

## Deferred (later cuts)

- **`plan scene scaffold`** — AI proposes a scene card from the chapter
  prose. The most complex P4 item; the CLI scene cards already cover
  authoring.
- **Tension model depth** — per-scene tension, AI-rated intensity as an
  `analyze`-tier overlay (the curve stays deterministic by default).
- **Sequel cards** — reaction / dilemma / decision, the reactive
  counterpart to the proactive scene.

## Carryovers (still open)

- **The Whole-Book AI Editor** (RAG over the whole manuscript) → 1.4+.
- **1.2.20:** ePub inline images + popup footnotes.
- **Facts follow-ups (1.2.21):** internal-consistency check, series-shared
  facts.
- PDF follow-ups: N-up / booklet quick-impose presets; CMYK-JPEG grayscale.
- Sixth supported language; GitHub Release backfill for 1.2.11–1.2.19.

# Inkhaven 1.3.5 — Scene craft: scaffold, sequel, second opinion

_On top of 1.3.4. The Planning Board gained a scene grain in 1.3.4; 1.3.5
deepens it — AI **scene scaffold** (propose a card from the prose), **sequel
cards** (the reactive counterpart to the proactive scene), and a tension
**second opinion** (an AI intensity reading beside the deterministic curve).
Full plan: [PLANNING-4_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/PLANNING-4_PLAN.md)._

## Headline

- **Scene scaffold** — the cold-start problem: the prose already implies the
  goal/conflict/disaster, so the AI proposes them. CLI and TUI.
- **Sequel cards** — Swain's structure alternates proactive *scenes* with
  reactive *sequels* (reaction → dilemma → decision). The Board now models
  both halves.
- **Tension second opinion** — the deterministic curve counts open
  obligations; an opt-in AI pass rates *felt* intensity. Two independent
  readings catch more than one.

## Scene scaffold

You shouldn't type a scene's goal/conflict/disaster from scratch when the
chapter already implies them:

```sh
inkhaven plan scene scaffold --chapter the-wharf   # one chapter
inkhaven plan scene scaffold --all                 # every cardless chapter
```

It reads the chapter prose, asks the LLM for the dominant scene's
goal/conflict/disaster (3-tier `plan-scene-scaffold` prompt), and upserts the
card. In the **`Ctrl+V Shift+K`** scene board, **`g`** regenerates the
selected card — the proposal streams into the AI pane, and **`L`** files the
parsed result back into the card (the same lift used for the structural
analysis).

## Sequel cards

A scene is proactive (goal → conflict → disaster); a **sequel** is reactive
(**reaction → dilemma → decision**) — the disaster lands, the character
reels, weighs bad options, and decides, setting the next goal.

```sh
inkhaven plan sequel add "Mara reels" --chapter the-wharf \
    --reaction "she's gutted" --dilemma "pay or expose her father" \
    --decision "pay it quietly and hunt the truth"
inkhaven plan sequel list      # or `plan scene list` for both, kind-tagged
```

One unified card model: `Scene` gains a `kind` field (old scene cards load
unchanged — no migration). The weak-card check flips by kind — a scene with
no disaster doesn't *turn*; a sequel with no decision *stalls* — and once
sequels are in use, two scenes back-to-back flag the first's unprocessed
disaster. `plan check`, the `v` board, and `plan analyze` all show both
kinds.

## Tension second opinion

The 1.3.4 actual line is deterministic (open-obligation density). For an
independent reading:

```sh
inkhaven plan tension rate     # AI-rate each chapter's intensity 0–100
```

`plan check`'s TENSION section gains an `ai` column and the overlay a third
sparkline, so you compare three readings — **expected** (framework),
**actual** (obligations), **ai** (felt):

```
TENSION (expected vs actual vs ai intensity)
  Midpoint            expected  65%  actual  33%  ai  35% ⚠ flat
  Climax              expected 100%  actual 100%  ai  95%
```

When actual *and* ai both land low where the framework wants a peak, that's
two independent signals agreeing the middle sags. The ratings are cached
(`.inkhaven/tension-ai-<book>.json`, content-hash invalidated); the
deterministic curve stays the default, the `ai` line is opt-in.

## Under the hood

- Zero new dependencies — scaffold + the AI rating reuse the LLM stack;
  sequel cards reuse the scene write-back; the second-opinion line is a
  sidecar + a third sparkline.
- New pure, unit-tested helpers: `parse_scene_scaffold`, `parse_intensity`,
  the kind-branched `analyze_scenes` / `scene_body`, `AiTensionCache`.
- Tests 1317 → 1321. Tutorial 67 refreshed.

## Deferred (later cuts)

- **Multi-scene chapters** — scaffold proposes one card per chapter; splitting
  a chapter into several cards by scene break (`#`) is a later refinement.
- **Per-scene AI tension** — the second opinion is per-chapter.
- **The Whole-Book AI Editor** — still 1.4+.

## Carryovers (still open)

- **1.2.20:** ePub inline images + popup footnotes.
- **Facts follow-ups (1.2.21):** internal-consistency check, series-shared
  facts.
- PDF follow-ups: N-up / booklet quick-impose presets; CMYK-JPEG grayscale.
- Sixth supported language; GitHub Release backfill for 1.2.11–1.2.19.

# Inkhaven 1.3.6 — The Editorial Pass

_The capstone the 1.3 line has pointed at since 1.2.22 ("the substrate for
the 1.3 editorial-pass cycle"): unify every revision detector — the prose
ones AND the Planning Board's structure findings — into one ranked,
walkable, jump-to-location worklist. Full plan:
[EDITORIAL-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/EDITORIAL-1_PLAN.md)._

## Headline

Inkhaven has ~12 detectors. The problem was never detection — it was that
you ran each one separately (`doctor --scan`, `plan check`, `facts scan`, …)
and aggregated in your head. The Editorial Pass collapses all of it into
**one ranked worklist**, errors first, each finding you can jump to, defer,
or skip — the pre-submission sweep.

## `inkhaven edit`

```sh
inkhaven edit                      # the ranked worklist
inkhaven edit --json | jq '.errors'   # gate a CI build on zero errors
inkhaven edit --only structure,tension
```

Every finding carries a category, a severity (error → warn → info), a
location, and a message — unified from three sources:

- the editorial **`doctor`** classes (echo, pacing, continuity, naming,
  dropped-character, stalled-thread, numeric-contradiction, …),
- **`plan check`**'s structural findings (gaps, drift, pacing, flat tension,
  weak scenes / sequels),
- the **Facts-scan** sidecar (contradictions against your world facts).

The default pass is **deterministic** — it reads what's already computed,
runs no AI, and so works offline and in CI. `edit` is *manuscript
readiness*; `doctor` stays *project integrity* — they share the
author-judgment classes but aren't the same surface.

## The cockpit (`Ctrl+V Shift+R`)

The same worklist as a walkable modal:

- `↑↓` navigate; the selected finding's full message + hint expand below.
- `[` / `]` cycle the category filter.
- **`Enter`** jumps to the finding's chapter / paragraph in the editor (a
  `→` marks the jumpable ones). Most editorial findings are author judgment
  — the "fix" is you editing at the jumped-to spot.

### Skip and defer

- **`s`** skips a finding for the session.
- **`d`** **defers** it — persisted (`.inkhaven/editorial-dismissed.json`),
  fingerprinted by its text so it stays hidden until the prose changes
  (editing the passage renews it; a choice you've accepted stays gone).
- **`D`** clears every deferral.

From the CLI, deferred findings are hidden (with a count); `inkhaven edit
--show-deferred` includes them.

## The deep tier

The default reads the AI sidecars but never runs the AI. To refresh them
first — re-run the Facts scan, the tension scan, and the continuity
extract, then aggregate:

```sh
inkhaven edit --deep [--provider <name>]
```

A scan that can't run (no provider, an empty Facts book) is skipped and the
pass falls back to deterministic-only rather than aborting. `--deep` can't
combine with `--json`; for a CI gate, run the scans separately then
`inkhaven edit --json`.

## Under the hood

- Zero new dependencies — the pass *aggregates* existing detector outputs
  (no new detection), reuses the snapshot + open-by-uuid machinery, and the
  `--deep` tier reuses the existing scan commands.
- New pure, unit-tested code: `EditorialFinding` / `Location` / the
  per-source mappers / `aggregate` / the chapter extractor / the defer
  sidecar.
- The big new capability findings needed: **location resolution** (a file
  path or chapter title → a paragraph node id), so the cockpit can jump.
- Tests 1325 → 1326. One new tutorial (68).

## Deferred (later cuts)

- **AI rewrite-in-place** — "fix this echo / flat scene for me" (lift an AI
  rewrite into the buffer from a finding). A natural follow-up.
- **A TUI `--deep` trigger** — three sequential blocking AI passes don't
  belong in a modal key handler; run `edit --deep` in a terminal, then open

# Inkhaven 1.3.7 — Close the loop: AI rewrite-in-place

_On top of 1.3.6. The Editorial Pass *found* every problem and *jumped* you
to it — but the fix was still all manual. 1.3.7 turns the cockpit from a
navigator into an actor: `f` on a rewritable finding streams an AI rewrite

## Headline

The cockpit could drop your cursor on a flat sentence, an echo cluster, an
overlong paragraph — and then you were on your own. For the prose-level
findings, the AI can now propose the fix.

## `f` — rewrite-in-place

In the **`Ctrl+V Shift+R`** cockpit, a **`✎`** marks the rewritable findings:

- **echo** — rewrite the paragraph to vary the over-repeated word.
- **pacing** — tighten an overlong paragraph.
- **show-don't-tell** — rewrite a telling passage to show (new in 1.3.7 — see
  below).

Press **`f`**: it opens the finding's paragraph, streams a category-specific
rewrite into the AI pane, and pops the **diff review** — the same one the
1.2.11 sentence-rhythm rewrite uses. **`a`** snapshots the paragraph (the
original is one `F6` away) then replaces it; **`r`** discards. The judgment
categories (structure, continuity, a fact contradiction, a weak scene) stay
jump-only — there's no honest single-paragraph rewrite for "the midpoint
sags."

The rewrite prompt resolves through the usual three tiers (an
`editorial-fix-<category>` entry in the Prompts book → `prompts.hjson` →
built-in, multilingual), so the rewriting voice is yours to tune.

The marquee rewritable category wasn't yet an `edit` finding — show-don't-tell
lived only as a live editor overlay. 1.3.7 surfaces it: the same regex
detector now runs over every paragraph in `inkhaven edit`, emitting a
`show-tell` finding per telling phrase with a paragraph + char-range location
— jumpable and `f`-rewritable. No new detection; the regex already shipped.

# Inkhaven 1.3.8 — World consistency

_On top of 1.3.7. A long book builds a world — a climate, a geography, a
cast with fixed attributes, a setting in time — and the tools to keep that
world consistent were scattered. 1.3.8 fills the four remaining gaps: does
the world contradict *itself*, does the prose fit its *era*, can you *see*
the whole world at once, and can a *series* share one canon. Full plan:
[WORLD-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-1_PLAN.md)._

## Headline

`facts scan` already checked the prose against the Facts book and
`continuity-drift` caught a character's eyes changing colour. What it
couldn't do: notice when the Facts book disagrees with *itself*, flag a
wristwatch in an 1840 novel, show you the whole world on one screen, or let
Book II of a trilogy share Book I's canon. Now it can.

## `facts check` — internal consistency

`inkhaven facts check` runs an AI pass over the *whole* Facts book looking
for contradictions between the facts themselves — "winters are mild" under
Climate vs. "the harbor freezes each January" under Geography:

```
facts check: 1 internal contradiction(s):
  ⚠ winters are mild  ⟷  the harbor freezes each January
      ↳ a mild winter can't freeze a harbor
```

Cached in `.inkhaven/facts_check.json` (order-independent content hash),
`--json` for a CI gate. The findings also surface in the **Editorial Pass**
(`inkhaven edit`, category `world`) alongside everything else.

## Anachronism detection

Set the manuscript's setting `year` and Inkhaven flags terms that postdate
it — a "wristwatch" before 1900, a "telephone" before 1876, "okay" before
1839:

```hjson
editor: { style_warnings: { anachronism: {
  year: 1840
  terms: [ { term: "spyglass-cam", earliest: 1990 } ]
} } }
```

A ~35-term built-in lexicon ships (each with its earliest plausible year);
your `terms` add to it. Off until you set a `year` — a contemporary novel
sees nothing. Findings appear in `inkhaven edit` (category `anachronism`),
jumpable to the exact word.

## The story bible — `Ctrl+V Shift+L`

One chord (**L** for **L**ore) opens a consolidated, navigable view of the
world: every **Character** with the attributes `continuity extract` has
tracked across chapters beneath it (`eye_color: brown (ch.3)`), plus the
**Places**, **Artefacts**, and **Facts** books. `↑↓` navigate, **`Enter`**
jumps to an entry's source paragraph (a `→` marks the jumpable rows).

## Series-shared facts

Point a `facts.shared_path` at a directory of plain-text fact files (one
file per fact — filename is the title, contents the body) and a whole series
shares one canon:

```hjson
facts: { shared_path: "../series-bible/facts" }
```

`facts check` then layers the shared canon under each book's local facts
(**local wins** on a name clash). Or `inkhaven facts import` copies a
snapshot into this book's Facts book as paragraphs (idempotent, dry-run by
default, `--yes` to write, `--from <dir>` to override).

## Under the hood

- Zero new dependencies. The fact-check + import reuse the Facts-scan
  sidecar machinery (`io_atomic`, DefaultHasher content hash); the
  anachronism detector reuses the `style_warnings` per-line detector
  substrate; the story bible reuses the lexicon books + the continuity
  sidecar.
- New pure, unit-tested code: `FactCheckReport` / `parse_conflicts` /
  `shared_facts`, the `AnachronismDetector`, `editorial::from_fact_conflict`,
  the story-bible row builder.
- Tests 1328 → 1333. Tutorial 69 added.

and asks the model for just its replacement.

The last live-overlay detector not yet in `inkhaven edit`. Filter words
(intensifier crutches + hedges — `just`, `really`, `very`, `seemed`) now

# Inkhaven 1.4.1 — Chat with your book

_The AI pane's **Book** scope used to ship the entire manuscript with every question —
slow on a real book, and grounded in nothing. 1.4.1 replaces it with **retrieval-augmented
generation** (BOOK_RAG-1): a Book-scope question now retrieves the handful of paragraphs
that actually bear on it, grounds the answer in them, and makes the model **cite** them.
Built entirely on infrastructure already in the tree — the on-save vector index every
semantic feature uses — with **no new dependencies**._

_Plan: [BOOK_RAG-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/BOOK_RAG-1_PLAN.md) · New tutorial:
[87](../Tutorials/87-chat-with-your-book.md)_

## The change — Book scope is retrieval-augmented

Put the cursor in a manuscript book, cycle the AI pane to **Book** scope (**F9**), and ask
a question. Instead of sending the whole book, Inkhaven now:

1. **Retrieves** the most semantically relevant paragraphs (the same vecstore HNSW index
   that powers every other semantic search),
2. **Expands** each hit with a neighbouring paragraph or two so it reads in context,
3. **Token-budgets** the result into a focused grounding block, and
4. **Grounds** the answer in those passages — every claim about the book is a markdown
   citation, `[label](#id)`, pointing at the paragraph it came from.

If the model ever cites an id that wasn't in what it was given, Inkhaven flags it inline —
`[citation could not be validated: …]` — so a hallucinated reference can't pass as
grounded. When nothing in the book addresses a question, the model is told to say so
plainly rather than confabulate.

This is **always on** for Book scope — there is no toggle and no "send the whole book"
fallback. **The other scopes are unchanged:** Selection, Paragraph, Subchapter, and
Chapter still send exactly the text they name.

### See what it retrieved

Above the conversation, a collapsed line shows how many passages grounded the answer —
**`p`** expands it (and `p` again collapses), listing each passage's similarity score, a
**★** for a direct hit, its breadcrumb, and its opening. Retrieval happens **once per chat
session**: follow-ups reason over the same passages; clearing the chat history re-grounds
the next question. Save an edited paragraph while a Book conversation is open and Inkhaven
nudges you once — *"book changed since retrieval — clear chat to re-ground on the new
text"* — a reminder, never an interruption.

### What's in scope

Retrieval is always anchored to the user book the cursor is in. Because a question about
your story often wants your *notes* about the story, a curated set of author-content
system books joins the pool — **Notes, Research, Places, Characters, Artefacts, World,**
and **Language** by default — while the internal/meta books (Scripts, Prompts, Typst,
Help, Intent) never enter retrieval. All of it is tunable in the new **`book_rag:`**
config block (`top_k`, `context_expansion`, `max_context_tokens`,
`include_system_books` / `exclude_system_books`).

## From the terminal — `inkhaven book-rag`

**`inkhaven book-rag retrieve <query>`** inspects exactly what Book-scope chat would
ground on — no LLM call, no cost:

```sh
inkhaven book-rag retrieve "what does Mara fear about the voyage?"
inkhaven book-rag retrieve "the harbour market" --top-k 8 --context
```

`--book-name` selects the book in a multi-book project, `--top-k` overrides the config for
that run only, and `--context` prints the literal grounding block the model would receive
instead of the human-readable listing. The CLI and the pane share one retrieval core, so
what you see is what grounds the chat.

## From a script — `ink.book_rag.*`

Eight new **read-only** Bund words expose the same retrieval to scripts (also aliased
`book_rag.X`):

| Word | Stack | What it does |
|------|-------|--------------|
| `ink.book_rag.retrieve` | `( anchor query -- passages )` | passage dicts `{id, breadcrumb, body, score, is_hit}` |
| `ink.book_rag.context` | `( anchor query -- text )` | the composed grounding block |
| `ink.book_rag.scope` | `( anchor -- ids )` | the node ids in the retrieval pool |
| `ink.book_rag.config` | `( -- dict )` | the active `book_rag` config |
| `ink.book_rag.system_prompt` | `( lang -- text )` | the localized grounding prompt |
| `ink.book_rag.estimate_tokens` | `( text -- n )` | rough token estimate (≈ chars/4) |
| `ink.book_rag.cited_ids` | `( passages -- ids )` | the valid-citation set |
| `ink.book_rag.validate_citations` | `( response ids -- text )` | flag hallucinated `](#id)` citations |

An *anchor* is any node's slug-path; retrieval runs against the user book it belongs to.
All eight gate under `store_read` (default-allowed): the retrieval is local, nothing
mutates, and no LLM is called. See [BUND_TUTORIAL.md](../Bund/BUND_TUTORIAL.md).

## Multilingual

The grounding contract — cite the passages, admit when they're silent — ships localized
for the five baseline languages (English, Russian, Spanish, French, German), selected by
the active prompt language and falling back to English for any other. Answers come back in
the language you ask in.

## Cost

Each Book answer is one local retrieval plus one grounded model call — far less than
shipping the whole manuscript. Those calls are tagged under the **`book_rag`** category in
`inkhaven cost` / **`Ctrl+B $`**, so you can see what chatting with your book costs. True
to Inkhaven's permissive principle, that figure **informs; it never blocks** a question.

## Dependencies & compatibility

**No external application or binary dependencies; no new runtime crates** — BOOK_RAG-1 is
built entirely on the existing `.typ` prose, DuckDB store, Fastembed embeddings, and the
vecstore HNSW index. The one behavioural change: **Book scope no longer sends the whole
book** — it retrieves and grounds instead. No on-disk shape moved; no config migration is
required (the `book_rag:` block is optional, every default preserving good behaviour).
Tests 1850 → 1855.

# Inkhaven 1.4.10 — Jinja template paragraphs

_Some content isn't free prose — it's **structured** and **data-driven**: a character sidebar that
should read the character's actual name and species, an endpoint table built from a list of fields,
a shared admonition written once. STRUCT-1 adds **Jinja template paragraphs**: a paragraph with
`content_type: "jinja"` is a [minijinja](https://docs.rs/minijinja) template the assembler renders
to **Typst** before `typst compile` runs — two layers, strictly sequential, never nested. It's
**self-gating** (no Jinja paragraphs, no change) and adds **one crate** (`minijinja`; its transitive
deps were already in the tree)._

_Plan: [STRUCT-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/STRUCT-1_PLAN.md)_

## Write a template

Put the tree cursor in one of your books and press **`e`** (mnemonic: t**e**mplate). You get a
`.jinja` paragraph — `⟡` glyph in the tree, `[jinja]` badge in the editor, Jinja syntax
highlighting — seeded with a starter that documents the variables you can use:

```jinja
= {{ title }}

#block[Edit this template. Link HJSON paragraphs with Ctrl+V a to populate `linked`.]
```

`{{ … }}` is an expression, `{% … %}` a statement, `{# … #}` a comment; everything else is plain
Typst, passed straight through.

## Pull in real data

The interesting variable is `linked`. Link an HJSON paragraph to your template with **`Ctrl+V a`** —
say a Characters entry `01-aria` with `{ name: "Aria", species: "fox" }` — and read its fields,
keyed by the linked paragraph's slug:

```jinja
= {{ linked["01-aria"].name }}

#block[A {{ linked["01-aria"].species }}.]
```

At assembly that renders to `= Aria` / `#block[A fox.]`. Change Aria's species in one place and
every template that reads her re-renders. You also get `title`, `slug`, `book.title`,
`chapter.title`, `language`, and `genre`.

## Share fragments via the Snippets book

A `.jinja` paragraph **in the Snippets book** (REUSE-1) becomes an includable template, named by its
tree path — `Snippets/Admonitions/warning` → `snippets/admonitions/warning.jinja`. Include it from
any manuscript template:

```jinja
{% include "snippets/admonitions/warning.jinja" %}
```

inkhaven registers every snippet template **before** rendering anything, so the include always
resolves — even a snippet that includes another snippet.

## Assemble

At Book assembly (**`Ctrl+B A`** / `inkhaven build`) inkhaven renders each Jinja paragraph to a
`.typ` in the assembled tree, then runs `typst compile`. The `{{ … }}` tags are gone by the time
Typst sees anything.

By default a render failure (bad syntax, missing include, typo'd variable) **aborts the whole
assembly** with the offending paragraph + error — CI-safe, no silently-dropped content. Set
`jinja.continue_on_error: true` to write a **visible** Typst error block in place and keep going.

## Convert an existing paragraph

`e` *creates* a fresh seeded template. To *convert* an existing leaf, cycle its type with **`t`** /
**`T`** in the Tree pane — the node-type morph gained a `jinja` rung:
`typst → hjson → jinja → bund`.

## Works in any language

The template receives `language`/`genre`, so you can branch yourself
(`{% if language == "ru" %}Глава{% else %}Chapter{% endif %}`); linked HJSON values (Cyrillic,
accented Latin, …) pass through verbatim.

## Also in this release

- **`#include` validator completeness (REUSE-1 polish).** The save-time snippet validator now also
  catches a **typo'd snippets directory** (`../nippets/<slug>.typ` whose filename matches a known
  snippet) and — once a book is assembled — verifies **generic** Typst `#include` paths resolve
  against the assembled output (not just snippet includes), while keeping the snippet-slug check as
  the pre-assembly path.

## Notes

- **Self-gating, additive:** no Jinja paragraphs → no behaviour change. **No new `NodeKind`, no
  `ChildRef` variant, no DuckDB schema change** — `content_type: "jinja"` on an ordinary paragraph,
  `.jinja` on disk. Jinja paragraphs are skipped by the Inner Editor, Inner Socrates, and the idle
  fact-checker (markup, not prose).
- **One new crate:** `minijinja` (in-memory template registration — no filesystem globs; its
  transitive deps were already present). Built on the existing `.typ` + DuckDB + serde-hjson stack.
- Orthogonal to the text-expansion snippet system (`tui/snippets.rs`): that injects a value as you
  type; Jinja paragraphs generate structured Typst at assembly. New tutorial 93. Tests 1936 → 1949.

# Inkhaven 1.4.11 — Structural paragraphs & deletion hardening

_Technical and nonfiction chapters aren't pure prose — they're prose interleaved with **code
listings, admonition boxes, math, procedures, and tables**. Inkhaven used to treat all of those as
ordinary paragraphs: same `¶` glyph, same Inner Editor style notes, all counted toward your word
total. STRUCT-2 lets you mark them for what they are — and hardens deletion so removing a chapter is
no longer a leap of faith. **Purely additive**: no new content type, no store change, **no new
dependencies.**_

_Plan: [STRUCT-2_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/STRUCT-2_PLAN.md)_

## Part A — Structural paragraph subtypes

Press **`i`** in the Tree pane and pick a subtype:

```
⌨  code listing
⚠  admonition: note / warning / tip / caution
∫  math
≡  procedure
⊞  table
```

You get a `.typ` paragraph with a type-specific tree glyph and the matching **Typst boilerplate
seeded** — a `#figure` code block, a coloured `#block` admonition, a `$ … $` equation, a `+`-step
procedure, or a `#table`.

The marker is a **`para:*` tag**, not a new content type. So a structural paragraph:

- shows its subtype glyph (`⌨ ⚠ ∫ ≡ ⊞`) instead of `¶`;
- is **skipped by the Inner Editor and Inner Socrates** — style and Socratic questions don't apply to
  a code block (procedures are the exception — steps are prose, so they still get feedback);
- is **excluded from the prose word count** — **Book Info** (`Ctrl+B I`) shows prose `paragraphs` and
  `structural` separately, so your word total reflects the writing.

Because it's just a tag, you manage it with the tag picker (**`Ctrl+B ]`**): add `para:table` to an
existing paragraph to make it structural, or remove it to turn it back into prose — the body never
moves, no morph cycle to walk.

## Part B — Deletion hardening

Deleting a chapter or book gained three recovery layers (`d` on a node):

1. **The confirmation shows the word count** — `Delete chapter `Act II` and 12 descendants (15,342
   words)?` — so you know what's at stake (omitted for zero-word deletes).
2. **Branch deletes are recoverable.** A chapter/book delete now stashes **every paragraph leaf**
   into the kill-ring (was single-paragraph only); **`Ctrl+B U`** restores them one at a time, in
   original order, and the status reports each one's word count. **`Ctrl+V Shift+U`** is the picker.
3. **Pre-delete snapshots.** Before a branch delete, inkhaven snapshots every paragraph
   (`pre-delete: <title> · <date>`), taken before the delete fires so it's safe even on partial
   failure — recover any of them from the **`F6`** picker long after the kill-ring has cycled.

Three layers: you see what you'll lose, you get instant undo, and you have a durable safety net.

## Notes

- **Purely additive, self-describing.** Structural type is a `para:*` tag on an ordinary `.typ`
  paragraph — **no new content type, no new `NodeKind`, no `ChildRef`, no DuckDB schema change.**
  A paragraph can be both `content_type: "jinja"` and `para:code` (the jinja gate fires first).
  Single-paragraph delete behaviour is unchanged.
- **No new dependencies.** Built on the existing tag system, the kill-ring, and the annotated-snapshot
  API. New tutorial 94. Tests 1949 → 1952.

# Inkhaven 1.4.12 — Narrative voice profiling

_A writer finishing chapter 40 of a long novel has no way to answer the question: does chapter 40
read like the person who wrote chapter 1? Sentence rhythm, hedging density, interiority, and sensory
balance are all measurable **without an LLM, without a parser, and without any external dependency** —
and nothing in Inkhaven measured them. NARR-1 fills that gap. `inkhaven prose` produces a
deterministic, chapter-ordered voice fingerprint for every book, stores it, exposes it via CLI and
Bund, and surfaces chapter-level drift as informational findings in the Output pane. It **measures;
it never prescribes.** Five languages are first-class: **EN, RU, DE, FR, ES.** **No new runtime
crates.**_

_Plan: [NARR-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/NARR-1_PLAN.md)_

## Profile your book

```sh
inkhaven prose profile          # compute + print the per-book voice profile
inkhaven prose profile --deep   # + Tier-2 (sensory balance, active/passive ratio)
```

The metrics, all deterministic:

- **Tier 1 (language-agnostic)** — sentence-length distribution (p10–p90),
  **coefficient of variation** (a falling CV across chapters = a voice narrowing), **burstiness B**,
  and **MATTR** (length-corrected lexical diversity).
- **Tier 1 (language-sensitive)** — **modal density** (epistemic hedging — broader than modal
  auxiliaries: German Konjunktiv II, French/Spanish conditional/subjunctive adverbs) and
  **interiority ratio** (free-indirect-discourse markers; German *erlebte Rede* particles reported
  separately).
- **Tier 2 (`--deep`)** — **sensory channel balance** (visual/auditory/olfactory/tactile/kinesthetic)
  and **active/passive ratio** (per-language detection).

Every language-sensitive metric has a complete curated word list for all five languages; a book in
an unsupported language still gets the full Tier-1 rhythm tier plus a note.

## See where the voice drifted

```sh
inkhaven prose drift                       # each chapter vs the baseline
inkhaven prose drift --mode rolling        # adjacent chapters
inkhaven prose drift --reference <project> # vs another project's book (a series)
```

Drift lists each chapter's ΔCV / ΔMATTR / Δmodal / Δinteriority plus the **threshold crossings** —
the metrics that moved past their configured limit vs the baseline chapter. `inkhaven prose suggest`
explains how to read each one.

## From the editor — `Ctrl+V V`

**`Ctrl+V V`** (Voice) runs the check in the **background** — **content-hash lazy**, so only the
chapter you just edited recomputes, and **zero-AI / zero-cost** (no provider, no budget). Any
threshold crossing lands in the **Output pane** as an informational `prose` finding that navigates
to the chapter. **`Ctrl+V Shift+V`** toggles **ambient** mode (off by default): re-run after an
editing pause, gated by a cooldown floor.

## Notes

- **Self-gating, zero-cost.** Nothing runs until you ask (CLI / `Ctrl+V V` / opt-in ambient); the
  background check never calls an LLM. Profiles live in a new `.inkhaven/prose.duckdb`, invalidated
  by a content hash; a language change recomputes only the language-sensitive metrics.
- **Scripting** — read-only `ink.prose.{profile,drift,violations,refresh}`; the `prose:` config block
  tunes the window / thresholds / language and accepts `extra_modal_tokens` for genre-specific
  hedging. Structural paragraphs (STRUCT-2) are reduced to prose; Jinja templates (STRUCT-1) excluded.
- **No new runtime crates.** Built on the existing `.typ` + DuckDB + `regex` stack. New tutorial 95.
- Also: the **Output pane** gained `Home` / `End` / `PageUp` / `PageDown` navigation.
- Tests 1952 → 1996.

# Inkhaven 1.4.13 — The manuscript Outline

_The side Tree pane is a navigator: narrow, always a keystroke away, good for jumping to a paragraph.
But when you want to **restructure** a book — drag a scene to another chapter, reorder beats, promote
an aside into its own section — a thin sidebar fights you. OUTLINE-1 adds a **full-screen, foldable
Outline** of the whole manuscript with structural editing built in: reorder, promote/demote, and
**cross-parent paragraph copy/move**. Everything has CLI and Bund parity, and every mutation runs on
the same filesystem-aware store primitives the Tree pane uses, so the two stay in lock-step. **No new
runtime crates.**_

_Plan: [OUTLINE-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/OUTLINE-1_PLAN.md)_

## Open it

Press **`Ctrl+2`** to open the Outline full-screen. If your terminal re-encodes `Ctrl+2` as NUL or
`Ctrl+@` (many do), the reliable backup is **`Ctrl+B Shift+O`**. `Ctrl+T` now focuses the side **Tree**
pane.

The Outline opens with Books and Chapters expanded and everything deeper folded — a structural
overview you drill into. Its view state (folds, cursor, scroll, filter) persists per project to
`.inkhaven/outline-state.json`, so it reopens exactly where you left it. When the window is ≥ 80
columns wide, a **detail panel** on the right shows the cursor node's title, kind, ancestor
breadcrumb, status, word count vs target (or child count for branches), tags, and last-modified date.

## Navigate, fold, restructure

```
j / k   ↓ / ↑          move                 Enter / l / →   expand (or step in)
g / G                  first / last         h / ←           collapse (or step out)
Space                  toggle a fold        / + type        filter
Shift+J / Shift+K      reorder siblings     < / >           promote / demote one level
```

**Reorder** swaps two siblings (renaming their `NN-` filesystem prefixes for you). **Promote** (`<`)
lifts a node up a level — appending it under its grandparent; **demote** (`>`) nests it into the
preceding sibling. These act on childless nodes (paragraphs and leaves); branch restructuring stays in
the Tree pane. A move that would break the hierarchy rules leaves the manuscript untouched and explains
why in the status line.

## Copy and move a paragraph across chapters

A shared clipboard spans the Outline **and** the Tree pane:

```
y   copy the cursor paragraph     m   move (cut) it     f   affix it
```

`f` lands the held paragraph as the **last child of the target's effective parent** — INTO the target
when it's a branch, alongside it when it's a paragraph. **Move** relocates and clears the clipboard;
**copy** duplicates (fresh uuid, prose metadata carried — tags, status, target, links — but **not** any
timeline event, so you never mint a duplicate event) and stays held for repeat pastes. The Outline
footer shows what's held: `[move: harbour-scene]`.

## Filter

Press **`/`** and type. The Outline collapses to the **path-to-match tree** — every node whose title or
slug matches, plus its ancestors, so you see matches in context. Matching is case-insensitive and
**Unicode-aware** (it works in Russian, French, German…). `Enter` applies; `Esc` is **staged** — exit
editing → clear the filter → save the view state and close.

## From the terminal and from Bund

Full parity:

```sh
inkhaven outline [--filter <s>]                 # print the tree as text
inkhaven paragraph copy <src> <dest>            # cross-parent duplicate
inkhaven paragraph move <src> <dest>            # cross-parent relocate
```

`src` / `dest` are the slash-separated slug paths printed by `inkhaven outline`. Bund: `ink.outline.print`
( `-- text` ), `ink.outline.paragraph_copy` ( `src dest -- uuid` ), `ink.outline.paragraph_move`
( `src dest --` ) — the two mutators need the `store_write` category enabled.

## Notes

- **One implementation, four surfaces.** The Outline pane, the Tree-pane clipboard, the CLI, and the
  Bund words all run on the shared `store::{move_node_to_parent, copy_paragraph_to_parent}` primitives
  (and `swap_siblings` for reorder), so however you reach for a move, it behaves identically and stays
  filesystem-correct (directories renamed, `NN-` prefixes reassigned, descendant `file` paths rewritten).
- **Childless-only reparenting, on purpose.** Promote/demote and paragraph move operate on childless
  nodes. A *branch* move would also have to rewrite every descendant's stored `path` depth-key — that's
  the Tree pane's domain and out of scope here.
- **Activation.** `Ctrl+2` (and its `Ctrl+@` / NUL re-encodings) opens the Outline; `Ctrl+B Shift+O` is
  the rebindable backup (`outline.open`). `Ctrl+T` keeps focusing the side Tree pane.
- **No new runtime crates; no new `NodeKind` / `ChildRef` / DB tables.** One additive sidecar
  (`.inkhaven/outline-state.json`, excluded from backup) and two new store methods.
- New tutorial 96. Tests 1996 → 2005.

# Inkhaven 1.4.14 — Dialogue quality & attribution

_Dialogue is the most technically demanding prose mode: readers must always know who is speaking,
said-bookisms (`he ejaculated`) degrade the page, and an unbroken run of talking heads loses the
physical scene. Inkhaven's Inner Socrates flagged unattributed dialogue in passing; nothing measured
dialogue as a **mode** with its own properties. DIALOG-1 does — **deterministically, with no LLM, no
parser, and no external dependency** — in five languages (EN/RU/DE/FR/ES) across three structurally
distinct quotation conventions. It **measures; it never prescribes.** **No new runtime crates.**_

_Plan: [DIALOG-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/DIALOG-1_PLAN.md)_

## Scan a book

```sh
inkhaven dialogue scan
```

```
Dialogue scan — `The Sunken Throne` [en]
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  dialogue spans detected   34
  zero attribution          3
  talking-head sequences    1
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  [ch.12 · 7f1a…] unattributed speech — no tag or character name within range
  …
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

`scan` **exits non-zero** when any zero-attribution span is found, so it doubles as a pre-submission
gate (`inkhaven dialogue scan --findings zero-attribution || …`). Three deterministic findings:

- **Zero-attribution** — a speech span with no tag or nearby character name. An established
  two-speaker exchange is allowed to alternate untagged for a run (default 8 turns) before it fires.
- **Said-bookism density** — a chapter whose non-neutral tag verbs (`whispered`, `growled`) run above
  the book's own baseline by more than a threshold.
- **Talking heads** — a run of dialogue-only paragraphs with no action beat (a ≥ 8-word line of
  narration) to ground the scene.

## Three quotation conventions

Detection is **not** uniform across languages — that's the heart of DIALOG-1:

- **EN, DE** — paired quotation marks (`"…"`, `„…"`, `»…«`).
- **FR, RU** — guillemets `«…»` and em-dash openers (`— …`); the French inline *incise*
  (`, dit-il,`, with the euphonic `-t-`) is stripped from the speech before it's measured.
- **ES** — all three, detected additively and de-duplicated.

Said-bookism and neutral tag-verb lists are embedded for all five languages in their dominant
narrative tense (EN past · RU perfective gender pairs · DE Präteritum · FR passé simple · ES
pretérito); EN adds a stem fallback so `whispering` matches `whispered`.

## Per-character fingerprints

```sh
inkhaven dialogue profile
```

```
Character    Utts  Avg words  MATTR  Questions  Excl.  Hedging
Mara           47      11.3   0.74      0.31    0.08    0.019
Aldric         83      11.8   0.69      0.12    0.22    0.041
```

Each character gets a six-metric voice signature — utterance count, average length, vocabulary
diversity (MATTR), question / exclamation ratios, hedge density — built **only** from confidently
(`Certain`) attributed lines, reusing NARR-1's MATTR and modal word list. In the editor,
**`Ctrl+V Shift+Q`** opens the fingerprint view for the nearest character (one named in the open
paragraph, else the most-speaking) as ASCII bars with a compare line.

## In the editor

The dialogue check rides the **unified review pass** — **`Ctrl+B Shift+C`** runs it alongside the
fact / Socratic / timeline checkers; the findings land in the **Output pane** (navigable to the
flagged paragraph). Zero-AI and content-hash lazy, so only the chapter you just edited re-detects.
There's also a new Inner Socrates persona, **`theatergoer`** (`Ctrl+B J → S` to cycle to it): it
reads a dialogue scene as if the narrator's private glosses were invisible, and asks whether the
subtext is legible from the words and visible action alone.

## Notes

- **One implementation, four surfaces.** The pipeline, CLI, Bund, and TUI all run on the same
  detection / attribution / `dialogue.duckdb` core. Findings stay informational; profiles live in
  `.inkhaven/dialogue.duckdb`, invalidated by a content hash.
- **`dialogue:` config** tunes the windows / thresholds and — importantly for SF/fantasy — lets you
  mark genre speech verbs neutral (`extra_neutral_verbs: ["transmitted", "sent"]`) so telepathy
  isn't counted as a said-bookism.
- **Scripting** — read-only `ink.dialogue.{stats,fingerprint,violations,spans,refresh}` (refresh
  writes only the derived cache, so it stays `store_read`, like `ink.prose.refresh`).
- **No new runtime crates; no new system books; no new `NodeKind`.** One new
  `.inkhaven/dialogue.duckdb`, one new Inner Socrates persona (15 total), one new chord. Imports
  NARR-1's `ProseLanguage` + modal lists. New tutorial 97.
- Tests 2005 → 2039 (the engine is unit-tested across detection / attribution / store / pipeline /
  fingerprints; the CLI / Bund / TUI surfaces were validated end-to-end on real projects).

# Inkhaven 1.4.15 — Utopian/dystopian coherence checker

_Inkhaven's world-consistency stack (WORLD-4/5) checks **physical** and **temporal** facts. It does
not check the **logical coherence of a social premise**. A utopia or dystopia makes a structured
claim — *society organised this way produces these outcomes* — and utopian fiction fails not from plot
holes but from **coherence holes**: the mechanism doesn't scale to enforce the premise, two
consequences contradict, or a scene depends on something the premise eliminated. WORLD-6 adds a
three-stage checker for exactly that. It reads **only what you declare**, reasons about
**logical/systemic** structure only (never morality — reserved for a future Inner Theologian), and
grounds the `utopian-architect` Inner Socrates persona with what it finds. **No new runtime crates.**_

_Plan: [WORLD-6_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/WORLD-6_PLAN.md)_

## Declare a premise in the World book

Write your premise set in the **World** system book as paragraphs carrying the four new
`para:utopia-*` tags (add a tag with **`Ctrl+B ]`**):

| Tag | Glyph | Means |
|---|:--:|---|
| `para:utopia-premise` | ⊢ | what's different from the real world, and why |
| `para:utopia-mechanism` | ⚙ | how the premise is enforced / maintained |
| `para:utopia-consequence` | ⇒ | what the premise produces |
| `para:utopia-elimination` | ∅ | what the premise rules out |

Consecutive tagged paragraphs form one **premise group**; a gap breaks the group (a
`// world:group:<name>` comment names the next one), so a book with a dominant society *and* a
resistance can declare both.

## Run the check

```sh
inkhaven world utopia-check              # Stage 1 (extraction) — cheap
inkhaven world utopia-check --stage 2    # + pairing (chain logic) — explicit
inkhaven world utopia-check --stage all  # + per-chapter entailment scan
inkhaven world utopia-model              # the extracted claims, no checks
```

- **Stage 1** extracts your claims (one call per group).
- **Stage 2** checks claim pairs for logical compatibility (premise→mechanism,
  mechanism→consequence, consequence↔consequence) and raises **CHAIN BREAK**, **CONSEQUENCE GAP**, and
  **INTERNAL CONFLICT** findings. It's O(pairs) LLM calls, so it's **explicit-only** — never silent.
- **Stage 3** scans each chapter against the **elimination inventory** and flags **ENTAILMENT
  VIOLATION**s — prose that uses something declared eliminated.

`utopia-check` exits **1** on any chain-logic finding and **2** on any entailment violation, so it
doubles as a pre-submission gate. After Stage 1, a deterministic (no-LLM) pass cross-references the
elimination inventory against your **Facts** book: a fact that's also declared eliminated raises a
`Factual` finding to reconcile.

## In the editor

The cached findings surface in the Output pane via the **`Ctrl+B Shift+C`** review pass — read-only,
zero-cost (the LLM stages run only when you ask, on the CLI). The **`utopian-architect`** Inner
Socrates persona (`Ctrl+B J → S` to select it) opens its Slow session grounded by these findings,
naming the unresolved tensions before its questions begin.

## Deliberate tensions

If a contradiction is the point — surveillance *and* flourishing, the novel's central irony —
suppress it: `inkhaven world utopia-suppress --finding <id> --reason "…"`, or add a
`deliberate_tension` entry covering `utopia_coherence` to the magic ledger. Suppressed findings leave
the Output pane but stay recorded.

## Notes

- **`inkhaven world` is now a subcommand group** (`utopia-check` / `utopia-model` / `utopia-suppress`
  / `utopia-refresh`). The bare **`inkhaven world`** consistency snapshot — and `--deep` / `--entity`
  / `--json` — behave exactly as before; backward-compatible.
- **Scope is enforced in the prompts:** every stage reads only what you declared and judges only
  logical/systemic compatibility. Moral, spiritual, and historical-plausibility judgements are out of
  scope. The schema reserves a `theological` finding domain and `research` grounding hooks for future
  features, with no coupling.
- **Scripting** — read-only `ink.utopia.{model,findings,violations}`; `ink.utopia.suppress` mutates.
- **No new runtime crates; no new system books; no new `NodeKind`.** One new
  `.inkhaven/utopia.duckdb`, four new `para:utopia-*` tags, one `utopia:` config block. New tutorial
  98. Tests 2039 → 2069 (the deterministic surface — tag/group detection, store, prompt construction,
  JSON parsing, pair selection, Facts cross-reference, grounding text — is unit-tested; the live LLM
  stages are integration-only, like Inner Editor's engage).

# Inkhaven 1.4.16 — Character arc tracking

_Inkhaven already tracks two things about a character: the **facts** the continuity bible records, and
the **speech** DIALOG-1 fingerprints. CHAR-1 adds the third axis — **change over time**. Per named
character: a chapter-ordered chain of their observable state, a deterministic *agency* score, and
completeness checks against the arc you declared. A character arc is a promise — *this person starts
here, and the book earns them to there* — and CHAR-1 measures whether the manuscript keeps it. It
reads only your manuscript and your declarations, never edits your prose, and the only LLM pass is the
state extraction. **No new runtime crates.**_

_Plan: [CHAR-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/CHAR-1_PLAN.md)_

## Declare the arc

In the **Characters** system book, give a character an arc by adding a `character_arc` block to their
paragraph (HJSON, alongside any other metadata):

```hjson
character_arc: {
  arc_type: positive_change      // flat | corruption | fall | disillusionment (+ aliases)
  desired_state_start: "Defers to her family in every decision."
  desired_midpoint_state: "Begins to act without asking permission."   // optional
  desired_state_end: "Chooses for herself, against her family's wishes."
}
```

The five `arc_type`s are the structural arcs (Scrooge / Atticus / Michael Corleone / Macbeth /
Javert); aliases like `redemption`, `growth`, `steadfast` map in, and any other string falls back to a
generic completeness probe. Only the start and end are required.

## The two passes

**Agency** is deterministic and zero-AI. For each chapter a character appears in, inkhaven scores
`active / (active + passive)` presence with a windowed name↔action-verb heuristic — a name *before* an
action verb (with no other character between) reads as active; a name *after* the verb, or the subject
of a passive construction, reads as passive — gated by NARR-1's passive detection. Five first-class
languages (EN/RU/DE/FR/ES), keyed off your project language.

**State extraction** is the only LLM pass. Chapter by chapter, with the previous chapter's summary fed
forward, it summarises what the character's behaviour, speech, and reactions *demonstrate* — observable
state only, never invented psychology — and flags whether something durably changed. Content-hash
lazy: editing one chapter re-extracts from there forward, nothing else. The chain is enriched with
DIALOG-1 utterance/hedge and NARR-1 interiority signals when those stores exist.

## Run it

```sh
inkhaven character refresh        # agency (instant) + state extraction (LLM)
inkhaven character check          # arc-completeness checks → exit 1 / 2 (CI gate)
inkhaven character plan           # Planning-Board coverage gaps (instant)
inkhaven character arc <name>     # the full report for one character
```

`check` runs four LLM checks per declared arc — start / midpoint / end alignment, and **arc earned**
(is the ending prepared, or merely asserted?) — plus a deterministic **stall** check (a long run of
unchanged chapters, with the chapter range and average agency). It exits **2** if the ending or the
earned-arc check fails, **1** on any other gap or stall. `plan` exits **1** if a declared arc has no
scene card, sits only in the first half, or never reaches the final act.

## In the TUI

- **`Ctrl+V Shift+N`** opens the **character arc view** for the nearest character (one named in the
  open paragraph, else the first tracked one): the declaration, the chapter state chain (✦ marks a
  change, with each chapter's agency), the arc checks, and any planning gaps. Read-only; `↑↓` scroll,
  `Esc` closes. Mnemonic: **N** for the arc, the bend (plain `n` is next-diagnostic).
- The **`Ctrl+B Shift+C`** review pass folds in the deterministic layers (agency + planning gaps +
  stalls) and surfaces the cached arc-check problems under the Output **`character`** category —
  zero-cost, no provider needed. The LLM checks stay explicit on the CLI.

## Notes

- **Scripting** — read-only `ink.char.{arc,stalls,checks,plan,refresh}` (the last two recompute only
  the deterministic cache).
- **Config** — the `char:` block tunes the stall threshold, agency windows, minimum chapters before
  LLM checks, the enrichment toggles, the language override, and `extra_action_verbs` for genre verbs
  the agency scorer should treat as deliberate action.
- **It never edits prose.** Findings are advisory; the cap informs, never blocks.
- **No new runtime crates; no new system books; no new `NodeKind`.** One new `.inkhaven/char.duckdb`,
  one `char:` config block, one new chord. New tutorial 99. Tests 2069 → 2103 (the deterministic
  surface — taxonomy, verbs, agency, store, planning gaps, prompt construction, JSON/check parsing —
  is unit-tested; the live LLM passes are integration-only, like Inner Editor's engage).

# Inkhaven 1.4.17 — The startup haiku

_Every time Inkhaven opens, you sit down to make something. The blank-page moment is real. HAIKU-1
puts a small, hand-curated poem in the Output pane to meet it — and gives the pane its first piece of
**good news** (until now it spoke only in warnings, findings, and task completions). It is the
simplest feature in Inkhaven: **no AI, no network, no generation.** All 25 poems (five per language,
EN/RU/DE/FR/ES) are hand-written and baked into the binary — present in the first millisecond of
startup, before the database journal replays, even on an airgapped machine. **No new crates.**_

_Plan: [HAIKU-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/HAIKU-1_PLAN.md)_

## Three moments

- **Startup** — one haiku lands in the Output pane when the project opens.
- **A new manuscript paragraph** — the instant you create a prose paragraph in a *user book* and open
  it to write, a fresh haiku meets you in the blank buffer. (Only real manuscript prose: never
  Characters/Places/Notes entries, Dictionary/Sources/Glossary/Snippets/Threads, or
  structural/template paragraphs.)
- **On demand — `Ctrl+Z p`** — when you want the pocket of stillness mid-session, press `Ctrl+Z p`
  (P for Poem). The status bar confirms `✦ haiku written to Output`; your focus doesn't move.

The poem is in the book's language (`editor.language`); an unsupported language falls back to English.
A per-process rotation (seeded from the clock so each launch differs) advances on every trigger, so
you rarely see the same poem twice in a session.

## What you'll see

A `✦ haiku` row in the Output pane with the three lines beneath it:

```
✦ haiku
   Blank page catches light —
   the sentence that wants writing
   waits inside the pen.
```

Only the most recent haiku ever lives in the pane — a new one quietly replaces the last, so they never
pile up. Each language carries three **Tier-A** poems (the manuscript — ink, the blank page, the first
sentence) and two **Tier-B** poems (the writer's surroundings — rain on the glass, a lamp's circle,
the pause between words); the Tier-A poems come first in rotation.

## Turning it off

```hjson
{ editor: { startup_haiku: false } }
```

That silences the startup and new-paragraph moments. The `Ctrl+Z p` chord still works whenever you
want one.

# Inkhaven 1.4.18 — Inner Theologian + the Thoughts pane

_Fiction carries moral weight. Every narrative makes claims — about what suffering means, whether
goodness is possible, what people owe each other, what transformation costs — and most are implicit.
Inkhaven's Inner family had two members (Inner Socrates for logical structure, Inner Editor for craft);
1.4.18 adds the third axis, **moral and theological seriousness**, and a new **Thoughts pane** to give
its long reflective output a proper home. **No new runtime crates.**_

_Plans: [INNER-THEOLOGIAN-1_PLAN.md](../PROPOSALS/INNER-THEOLOGIAN-1_PLAN.md)_

## Inner Theologian — a tradition-neutral comparativist

Inner Theologian reads any manuscript through the lenses of **eleven** moral and theological traditions
— Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox, Gnostic, LDS, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, and
secular moral philosophy — **not to judge the work by any of them, but to ask what each of them sees.**
It belongs to no tradition, advocates none, **never delivers a verdict**, and never edits your prose.
Every output is a question.

### Two tracks

**Fast track — deterministic, zero-AI.** Three `info` signals over your prose, in the Output
`theologian` category (the `⚖` glyph), folded into the `Ctrl+B Shift+C` review pass:

- **moral invisibility** — a named character harms another with no acknowledgment in the next few paragraphs;
- **consequence gap** — lethal or severe violence with no depicted consequence;
- **sacred levity** — sacred/ritual vocabulary sharing a paragraph with comic markers (the most cautious detector).

Five languages (EN/RU/DE/FR/ES), tradition-neutral word lists, none ever above `info`.

**Slow track — the LLM session.** Press **`Ctrl+B J → T`** to engage the open paragraph. It runs in
**two passes**: a *discovery* call decides which of all eleven lenses genuinely illuminate this
passage (and which are tellingly **silent** — a moral question the work never raises), then an
*analysis* call poses two to four questions through the chosen lenses, **in the book's language**,
always naming which tradition raises which and inviting you to say a lens is irrelevant ("that's useful
information too"). Grounded by WORLD-6 theological findings, CHAR-1 belief arcs, and in-scope signals
when present; each degrades cleanly.

### From the terminal

```sh
inkhaven theologian scan                       # the fast-track signals (exit 1 if any)
inkhaven theologian session --chapter 7        # a slow-track session over chapter 7
inkhaven theologian session --category 6       # the book's implicit theology (the broadest)
inkhaven theologian session --lens gnostic     # pin one tradition lens (skips discovery)
inkhaven theologian suppress --para <id> --reason "the banality of harm is the point"
```

Six question categories: **1** moral weight & consequence, **2** theodicy & innocent suffering,
**3** redemption & transformation, **4** sacred & transcendent, **5** duty & obligation, **6** the
work's implicit theology. Read-only `ink.theologian.{signals,suppress}` Bund; the `theologian:` config
block (windows, sub-budget, `disabled_lenses`, language); `.inkhaven/inner_theologian.db`.

## The Thoughts pane

**third right-side pane** — **Thoughts** — a read-only, scrollable, Markdown-rendered home for long
reflective output (the Inner Theologian slow track lands here).
